ocar.opportunity: Synapse-level connectomes of the fly visual system now show which developing neurons actually pair as partners, while cell-type transcriptomes and protein-binding maps list the adhesion molecules those cells express. Together those resources make it possible to hunt for receptor–ligand pairs that match neurons to their synaptic targets.
ocar.challenge: Developing neurites encounter many cell types and express large repertoires of cell-adhesion molecules, so identifying the pairs that actually specify wiring has been difficult. Closely related neurons that make different layer choices are especially informative but easy to lose in circuit complexity.
ocar.action: Yoo and colleagues, in Current Biology (2023), integrated a synapse-level Drosophila visual connectome with developmental expression and binding specificities of cell-adhesion molecules. They focused on genetically related T4/T5 motion-detection subtypes that choose alternative targets in adjacent neuropil layers.
ocar.resolution: Layer choice correlated with matching Beat and Side family receptor–ligand pairs in synaptic partners. Genetic tests showed that presynaptic Side-II and postsynaptic Beat-VI keep partners in the same layer; removing the pair disrupts layers and mis-targets presynaptic sites and postsynaptic dendrites.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose that different Side/Beat pairs work with other recognition molecules to set wiring specificity, and that combining transcriptomes, connectomes, and protein-interaction maps can identify further wiring determinants without prior bias.

summaries.beginner: As a fly’s brain is wired, each nerve cell must choose the right partners among many neighbors. This paper finds matching pairs of surface molecules that help related motion-sensing cells stay in the correct layer of the visual system.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2023), Yoo, Dombrovski, Zipursky, Kurmangaliyev and colleagues asked which cell-adhesion molecules match Drosophila visual neurons to their synaptic partners. They combined a synapse-level connectome of the motion circuit with developmental expression and known binding specificities, focusing on related T4/T5 subtypes that innervate adjacent layers. Matching Beat and Side receptor–ligand pairs tracked those layer choices. Removing Side-II and Beat-VI disrupted layers and sent axons and dendrites to the wrong places.
summaries.advanced: The genetic result is for one receptor–ligand pair (Side-II/Beat-VI) in T4/T5; other Beat/Side pairs are correlative pending similar tests. The strategy depends on genetically related neurons that make differential choices, so it may miss determinants used only by unrelated partners. Binding maps and expression are developmental snapshots and do not by themselves prove that a pair is used at the synapse in vivo.

plain_language_summary: As a fly’s brain is wired, each nerve cell must choose the right partners among many neighbors. This paper finds matching pairs of surface molecules that help related motion-sensing cells stay in the correct layer of the visual system.

ocar.opportunity: Basal animals offer independent evolutionary experiments in how integrative systems arise. Mapping both synaptic wiring and the chemical signaling that runs in parallel could explain how elementary cognition first appeared.
ocar.challenge: The mechanistic and evolutionary roots of animal cognition remain elusive. Dynamic chemical micro-environments—volume transmission by many signal molecules—are poorly measured, so links from cell-specific chemistry to behavior are hard to draw.
ocar.action: Moroz and Romanova, in Animal Cognition (2023), review evidence that neural and neuroid systems evolved more than once in basal metazoans, highlighting ctenophore nervous systems and neuroid-like systems in placozoans and sponges. They argue for uniting ‘chemoconnectomics’ with cellular analyses of behavior.
ocar.resolution: They treat a chemical connectome of hundreds of signal molecules, operating with or without classical synapses, as the most information-rich source of adaptability. Convergent evolution of integrative systems becomes a comparative framework rather than a single-origin story.
ocar.future_work: The authors call for new tools that link orchestrated, cell-specific volume transmission to behavior, using basal lineages as the foundation for studying origins of elementary cognition.

summaries.beginner: Thinking in animals depends on nerve cells, but similar control systems may have evolved more than once. This essay argues that chemical signals bathing tissues, not just wired contacts, are a major part of how simple animals coordinate behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In Animal Cognition (2023), Moroz and Romanova argue that animal neural and other integrative systems evolved convergently in basal metazoans, with striking examples in ctenophores, placozoans, and sponges. Besides synaptic wiring, they emphasize a chemical connectome of many signal molecules and volume transmission. They propose that ‘chemoconnectomics’ plus cellular behavior in these lineages is the way to study origins of elementary cognition. The review is conceptual: it frames a gap rather than reporting a new map.
summaries.advanced: No new connectome or chemical atlas is presented; claims about convergent origins and the primacy of chemical signaling are interpretive. Organism and method tags on the catalog row are empty, matching the essay’s phylogenetic breadth. Readers should treat ‘hundreds of signal molecules’ as a qualitative scale from the authors, not a counted inventory in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Thinking in animals depends on nerve cells, but similar control systems may have evolved more than once. This essay argues that chemical signals bathing tissues, not just wired contacts, are a major part of how simple animals coordinate behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section multibeam SEM can image cubic-millimeter-scale neural tissue at synapse-resolving detail, producing connectomes with morphology, synapses, and organelles. Aligning those petabyte volumes into navigable 3D is the step that makes the data usable.
ocar.challenge: A single cubic-millimeter acquisition yields hundreds of millions of tiles. Alignment must keep navigation smooth in all directions while not warping sections far from the original micrographs.
ocar.action: Watkins, Jelli and Briggman, in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2023), introduce msemalign, an alignment pipeline designed for scalability and simplicity on serial-section multibeam SEM volumes.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline can align petabyte-scale datasets with smooth transitions, while minimizing overall section distortion relative to the acquired images.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not report quantitative distortion metrics or a named production volume; applying the same distortion-minimizing alignment to additional multibeam SEM cubes is the natural next test.

summaries.beginner: To map a large piece of brain, microscopes take enormous numbers of tiny pictures that must be stitched into a 3D volume. This paper describes a software pipeline that lines those pictures up smoothly without stretching the tissue too far from how it was originally imaged.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2023), Watkins, Jelli and Briggman present msemalign for serial-section multibeam SEM. They note that ssmSEM is among the fastest routes to ~1 mm³ volumes at synapse-resolving resolution, but a cubic millimetre can produce hundreds of millions of tiles. The pipeline targets petabyte alignment with smooth 3D navigation while keeping section warps small relative to the raw micrographs. Catalog tags associate the work with mouse MICrONS-scale volumes and multibeam / serial-section EM.
summaries.advanced: The abstract is a methods claim about design goals (scalability, smoothness, minimized distortion) and does not give error statistics, runtime, or a named dataset result. ‘Hundreds of millions of tiles’ and ‘petabyte-scale’ are the authors’ scale statements; independent benchmarks against other EM aligners are not provided here.

plain_language_summary: To map a large piece of brain, microscopes take enormous numbers of tiny pictures that must be stitched into a 3D volume. This paper describes a software pipeline that lines those pictures up smoothly without stretching the tissue too far from how it was originally imaged.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomes already guide fly vision studies, but the lobula—thought to detect object-like features—is still under-mapped. Recovering its columnar inputs would let people hypothesize how lobula output neurons compute those features.
ocar.challenge: Available dense reconstructions mostly lack upstream visual neuropils that would normally identify lobula inputs. Incomplete input data has kept lobula connectomics underdeveloped.
ocar.action: Tanaka and Clark, in eNeuro (2022), clustered cells in a densely reconstructed Drosophila connectome by connectivity and morphology to extract candidate columnar inputs to lobula.
ocar.resolution: Clusters were homogeneous enough to look like real cell types and could be matched to previously identified types, revealing previously undocumented connectivity between lobula input and output neurons.
ocar.future_work: The authors state that more complete reconstructions are needed to verify these mappings, while offering the clusters as a basis for hypotheses about feature detection in lobula.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies compute object-like visual features in a brain region whose incoming wiring is still poorly listed. This study groups cells by shape and connections to guess which input types feed that region and how they contact the cells that send signals onward.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2022), Tanaka and Clark mapped columnar inputs to Drosophila lobula by connectivity- and morphology-based clustering on a dense EM reconstruction that mostly lacked other visual neuropils. The clusters were internally consistent and corresponded to known cell types, exposing previously undocumented input–output connectivity in lobula. They present the map as a hypothesis generator pending fuller reconstructions. The work uses electron microscopy in fly.
summaries.advanced: The authors themselves flag incomplete upstream neuropils as a source of identity error; cluster-to-type correspondence is therefore provisional. ‘Previously undocumented connectivity’ is claimed without numeric synapse counts in the abstract. Results should be read as connectivity hypotheses, not a verified input census.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies compute object-like visual features in a brain region whose incoming wiring is still poorly listed. This study groups cells by shape and connections to guess which input types feed that region and how they contact the cells that send signals onward.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila’s brain is small enough (roughly 200,000 neurons) yet behaviorally rich, and many experimental tools already exist. A near-complete EM connectome of chemical synapses is imminent, so an integrated model of the fly brain is a realistic near-term goal.
ocar.challenge: A wiring diagram of chemical synapses is not, by itself, an understanding of how the brain operates. It is unclear what additional data must be collected and organized on top of the connectome.
ocar.action: Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), itemize the measurements still needed—given what is known, what is underway, and what the EM connectome will soon provide—to build an integrated model of the D. melanogaster brain.
ocar.resolution: The paper is a requirements list rather than a new dataset: it frames the connectome as necessary but not sufficient and organizes remaining gaps for a whole-brain model.
ocar.future_work: The implied program is to obtain, collate, and organize the missing data classes they enumerate so that structure can be turned into a working model of the fly brain.

summaries.beginner: Scientists will soon have a detailed wiring diagram of the fruit-fly brain. This essay asks what else is still needed—beyond that diagram—before we can say we understand how the fly’s brain works.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Experimental Biology (2021), Scheffer and Meinertzhagen treat the forthcoming Drosophila EM connectome as a near-term opportunity: roughly 200,000 neurons, rich behavior, and many tools. They argue that an electron-microscopy description of neurons and chemical synapses is not enough for understanding. The paper inventories additional data required for an integrated brain model. It is a field-synthesis piece, not an empirical reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: The neuron count (‘roughly 200,000’) is the authors’ scale, not a census from this paper. The review addresses chemical synapses and does not resolve electrical synapses, neuromodulation, or extrasynaptic signaling in the abstract. What ‘understand the brain’ requires remains a programmatic list rather than a testable model.

plain_language_summary: Scientists will soon have a detailed wiring diagram of the fruit-fly brain. This essay asks what else is still needed—beyond that diagram—before we can say we understand how the fly’s brain works.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans connectomes exist at multiple developmental time points, so graph and motif tools can watch a nervous system’s network statistics change as the animal grows.
ocar.challenge: It is not obvious which graph invariants stay stable across development and which motifs grow or decay in unexpected ways.
ocar.action: Matelsky, Gray-Roncal and colleagues, in a 2021 bioRxiv preprint, applied graph and motif analysis to C. elegans connectomes across developmental stages and compared graph characteristics over time.
ocar.resolution: They report the evolution of the networks and highlight both stable invariants and patterns that grow or decay unexpectedly, offering a substrate for further analysis.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the changing motifs as a substrate rather than a finished developmental theory; linking unexpected growth or decay to specific behaviors or genes is left open.

summaries.beginner: The worm C. elegans rebuilds its wiring as it grows. This preprint compares network patterns at different ages to see which connection motifs stay put and which rise or fall.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Matelsky, Norman-Tenazas, Davenport, Reilly, and Gray-Roncal used graph and motif tools on C. elegans connectomes at multiple developmental time points. They compare graph characteristics and substructures over time, highlighting stable invariants and unexpectedly growing or decaying patterns. Catalog tags place the work on the White+ C. elegans dataset and graph analysis. Numeric motif counts are not given in the abstract.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the time points, the motif catalog, or statistical tests. ‘Unexpected’ growth or decay is qualitative. Results are a developmental comparison of graphs, not a claim that motifs cause behavioral change.

plain_language_summary: The worm C. elegans rebuilds its wiring as it grows. This preprint compares network patterns at different ages to see which connection motifs stay put and which rise or fall.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput 3D EM now lets the same cortical circuit be mapped at several postnatal ages, turning connectomics into a screen of how inhibitory innervation is built.
ocar.challenge: A comprehensive map of cortical inhibitory innervation during postnatal development had been missing, even as migration timelines and some molecular cues were known. Distinct target preferences (soma, apical dendrite, axon initial segment) might arise by different rules.
ocar.action: Gour, Helmstaedter and colleagues, in Science (2020), acquired 13 three-dimensional EM datasets from mouse barrel cortex layers 4 and 2/3 at postnatal days 5, 7, 9, 14, 28, and 56, and quantified inhibitory innervation of cell bodies, apical dendrites, and axon initial segments through the first four weeks.
ocar.resolution: Apical-dendrite preference is already nearly adult-like at P5. Soma-preferring axons acquire specificity from P5 to P9, with a peak of change between P7 and P9, when soma preference increased almost threefold and synapse density along those axons dropped almost twofold. Chandelier axons show first target preference by P14 and near-full specificity by P28; axo-axonic input to the axon initial segment grows from a minor fraction to about 50%.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest connectomic screening can next be used under genetic and environmental perturbations of circuit formation in mammalian cortex.

summaries.beginner: As a baby mouse’s cortex matures, inhibitory cells must attach to the right parts of other neurons. This study uses 3D electron microscopy at several ages to show that some attachments are almost adult-like from the start, while others are refined by removing misplaced contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2020), Gour, Boergens, Helmstaedter and colleagues mapped inhibitory synaptogenesis in mouse somatosensory (barrel) cortex with 13 3D EM volumes from P5 to P56, focusing on P5–P28. Apical-dendrite targeting is largely in place by P5. Cell-body innervation sharpens between P5 and P9, consistent with overabundance then removal of off-target synapses. Chandelier axons specialize later (preference by P14, near-complete by P28). Catalog tags include DS12 L4 barrel cortex, mouse, EM, and segmentation.
summaries.advanced: The P7–P9 ‘almost threefold’ soma-preference increase and ‘almost twofold’ drop in axonal synapse density are the abstract’s quantitative claims; chandelier AIS input reaching ‘~50%’ is likewise from this paper. Mechanisms (ab initio choice versus antispecific removal) are inferred from time series, not from live imaging of individual synapses. The screen is barrel cortex layers 4 and 2/3, not all cortex, and excitatory synaptogenesis is not the focus.

plain_language_summary: As a baby mouse’s cortex matures, inhibitory cells must attach to the right parts of other neurons. This study uses 3D electron microscopy at several ages to show that some attachments are almost adult-like from the start, while others are refined by removing misplaced contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Molecular biology, virology, microscopy, computing, and genetics have expanded the toolbox for mesoscale circuit tracing, letting experimenters label selected neuron populations and map their inputs and outputs.
ocar.challenge: Newcomers face an intersectional literature spanning fields they may not know, plus bottlenecks in analyzing and sharing tracing data.
ocar.action: Saleeba, McMullan and colleagues, in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2019), review mesoscale connectomic approaches from data collection to analysis, including a brief history, conventional and viral tracers, and methods for selecting neuronal subpopulations.
ocar.resolution: The review is written as a student’s guide: it surveys current reagents and notes weaknesses of widely used analysis and dissemination pipelines, plus likely trajectories of the technologies.
ocar.future_work: They highlight remaining bottlenecks in analysis and data sharing and the directions rapidly developing neuroanatomy tools are likely to take.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can follow the paths of selected groups of brain cells using dyes and viruses. This guide walks students through those tracing methods, how the data are analyzed, and where the field still struggles to share results.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2019), Saleeba, Dempsey, Le, Goodchild and McMullan review mesoscale mammalian circuit tracing for newcomers. After a short history of neuroanatomy they cover conventional and viral tracers, genetic selection of subpopulations, and analysis/dissemination bottlenecks. The piece sits at mesoscale (local and long-range population connections), not ultrastructural EM connectomics. Catalog tags include proofreading as a pipeline stage, reflecting annotation and QC of tracing data.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods survey, not a primary tracing dataset. ‘Mesoscale’ here means population-level anterograde/retrograde mapping, which should not be confused with synapse-resolution EM. Weaknesses of analysis pipelines are named qualitatively without benchmarks in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can follow the paths of selected groups of brain cells using dyes and viruses. This guide walks students through those tracing methods, how the data are analyzed, and where the field still struggles to share results.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-level optic-lobe connectomes, especially for ON-pathway T4 circuits, have already complicated the classic Hassenstein–Reichardt motion model. A single EM volume covering the whole optic lobe could put T4 and T5 inputs on the same footing.
ocar.challenge: OFF-pathway T5 knowledge was incomplete relative to T4. Reconstructing inputs across an entire optic lobe requires synapse prediction at a scale that earlier methods did not easily support.
ocar.action: Shinomiya, Plaza, Meinertzhagen and colleagues, in eLife (2019), built a connectome that integrates detailed connectivity for inputs to both T4 and T5 in one EM dataset of the entire Drosophila optic lobe, using automated synapse prediction suited to a large volume.
ocar.resolution: They corroborate prior T4 findings and comprehensively identify T5 inputs and receptive fields. The pathways share many features, consistent with an evolutionary link, but the authors also report differences and interactions that may explain distinct functional properties.
ocar.future_work: Those pathway differences and interactions become hypotheses for physiology: tests of whether the newly mapped T5 inputs account for OFF-edge motion selectivity distinct from T4.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies detect motion using two related visual pathways, one for bright edges and one for dark edges. This paper maps the incoming wiring of both pathways in one detailed dataset so they can be compared fairly.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019), Shinomiya, Huang, Scheffer, Plaza, Meinertzhagen and colleagues present a Drosophila optic-lobe EM connectome covering inputs to ON (T4) and OFF (T5) motion pathways in a single volume. Automated synapse prediction enabled reconstruction at this scale. T4 connectivity matches earlier reports; T5 inputs and receptive fields are identified comprehensively. Similarities suggest a shared evolutionary origin, while differences and cross-pathway interactions are proposed to underlie distinct physiology.
summaries.advanced: ‘Conclusive and comprehensive’ is the authors’ claim for this dataset; independent completeness metrics are not in the abstract. Novel reconstruction methods using automated synapse prediction are asserted without numeric precision/recall here. Functional properties are inferred from anatomy plus prior physiology, not new recordings in this paper.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies detect motion using two related visual pathways, one for bright edges and one for dark edges. This paper maps the incoming wiring of both pathways in one detailed dataset so they can be compared fairly.

ocar.opportunity: Dense voxel embeddings from deep metric learning can turn 3D EM images into a graph of affinities between voxels, which can then be partitioned into neurons.
ocar.challenge: Very thin processes and complex self-contact motifs cause systematic splits. A segmentation that is both high-precision on thin objects and able to agglomerate those splits is hard to obtain from a single representation.
ocar.action: Lee, Lu, Luther and Seung, in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (catalog year 2019), learn dense voxel embeddings with a convolutional network, build a metric graph including long-range repulsive edges, partition it, then reuse the same embedding net to agglomerate self-contact splits.
ocar.resolution: The initial partition has high precision with a substantial accuracy gain on very thin objects. The method is reported as state-of-the-art on 3D neuron reconstruction from serial-section EM, and the authors suggest the object-centered embedding may serve other automated circuit-reconstruction tasks.
ocar.future_work: They propose the representation as more generally useful for other computational tasks in automated neural circuit reconstruction, beyond the segmentation benchmark.

summaries.beginner: Computers must outline each nerve cell in a 3D microscope volume, including extremely thin branches that easily get cut into pieces. This paper teaches a network to place every tiny cube of the image in a map where pieces of the same cell sit close together, then groups them into whole cells.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (catalogued 2019), Lee, Lu, Luther and Seung use deep metric learning to produce dense voxel embeddings for 3D EM. A metric graph with long-range repulsive constraints is partitioned for a high-precision initial segmentation, especially improving thin objects. The same embedding network agglomerates systematic splits from self-contact motifs. They report state-of-the-art accuracy on serial-section EM neuron reconstruction. Catalog stages include preparation, sectioning, segmentation, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘State-of-the-art’ is asserted without named benchmark scores in the abstract. Self-contact agglomeration reuses the embedding net without modification, which is a design claim rather than an ablation table here. Serial-section EM anisotropy is implied by the problem setting; transfer to isotropic FIB-SEM is not demonstrated in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Computers must outline each nerve cell in a 3D microscope volume, including extremely thin branches that easily get cut into pieces. This paper teaches a network to place every tiny cube of the image in a map where pieces of the same cell sit close together, then groups them into whole cells.

ocar.opportunity: If an unsupervised image-to-image model could translate a new EM volume into the appearance of a dataset that already has labels, a segmentation network trained elsewhere might run without new ground truth.
ocar.challenge: Automated neuron reconstruction usually needs expensive, dataset-specific volumetric annotations. Domain shift between imaging methods and labs blocks naive reuse of trained models.
ocar.action: Januszewski and Jain, on bioRxiv (2019), enhance CycleGAN training with components from automated neuron segmentation, calling the method Segmentation-Enhanced CycleGAN (SECGAN).
ocar.resolution: In a zero-shot setting—segmentation trained only on volumetric labels from a different dataset and imaging method—they report near-perfect reconstruction accuracy on a benchmark connectomics segmentation dataset.
ocar.future_work: By reducing or eliminating novel ground-truth annotations, SECGANs are meant to lower a main practical barrier to automated reconstruction of new volume-EM datasets.

summaries.beginner: Teaching a computer to outline neurons usually requires people to label a new pile of images for every dataset. This preprint adds extra checks so an image-translation network can reuse labels from a different kind of microscope data.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Januszewski and Jain introduce Segmentation-Enhanced CycleGAN. They add segmentation-derived terms to unsupervised image-to-image translation so a model can adapt a new volume-EM dataset toward a labeled source domain. They report near-perfect accuracy on a connectomics segmentation benchmark in a zero-shot setting, with the segmenter trained only on another dataset and imaging method. Catalog tags include segmentation, proofreading, acquisition, and volume EM.
summaries.advanced: ‘Near perfect’ is not accompanied by a numeric score in the abstract. Zero-shot here means no new volumetric labels on the target, not that no source labels exist. CycleGAN training remains unsupervised on the target images; residual domain-shift failure modes are not enumerated here.

plain_language_summary: Teaching a computer to outline neurons usually requires people to label a new pile of images for every dataset. This preprint adds extra checks so an image-translation network can reuse labels from a different kind of microscope data.

ocar.opportunity: Anatomy of many fly visual circuits is known at high resolution, but molecular properties of those cell types are mostly unknown. Pairing cell-type transcriptomes with connectomes could identify transmitters, receptors, and shared molecular programs.
ocar.challenge: Measuring clean transcriptomes for many genetically accessed types, then interpreting noisy counts across a large catalog, is non-trivial.
ocar.action: Davis, Nern, Rubin, Eddy, Henry and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2018), used genetic driver lines, TAPIN-seq of intact nuclei, and a probabilistic interpretation method to profile Drosophila visual cell types.
ocar.resolution: They release high-resolution transcriptomes for 100 driver lines covering 67 cell types at http://www.opticlobe.com. Combined with reported connectomes, the resource supports identifying transmitters (including co-release), receptor-based functional hypotheses, and molecular commonalities across types.
ocar.future_work: The resource is intended for ongoing circuit-scale interpretation—matching more types brain-wide and turning receptor maps into physiological tests.

summaries.beginner: Knowing how fly visual cells are wired is not the same as knowing which chemical messages they send and receive. This preprint measures gene activity in dozens of identified cell types so those chemicals can be inferred.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2018), Davis, Nern, Picard, Reiser, Rubin, Eddy and Henry combine genetic access, TAPIN-seq, and probabilistic modeling to build transcriptomes for 100 Drosophila visual driver lines covering 67 cell types, hosted at opticlobe.com. They use the catalog with existing connectomes to assign transmitters, including co-release, and to generate receptor-based hypotheses. Catalog tags include fly and segmentation as a stream label. Numeric expression cutoffs are not in the abstract.
summaries.advanced: Driver lines are not identical to pure cell types; 100 lines covering 67 types implies some redundancy or mixed access. TAPIN-seq of nuclei may miss cytoplasmic RNA dynamics. Connectome pairing is interpretive: transmitter identity from expression is a prediction until physiology confirms co-release.

plain_language_summary: Knowing how fly visual cells are wired is not the same as knowing which chemical messages they send and receive. This preprint measures gene activity in dozens of identified cell types so those chemicals can be inferred.

ocar.opportunity: Automatically reconstructing synapses in EM would speed connectome building and plasticity studies and reduce manual validation.
ocar.challenge: Existing detection and segmentation methods were not adequate for accurate synaptic connectivity and did not sufficiently lighten validation.
ocar.action: Xiao, Han and colleagues, in BMC Bioinformatics (2018), built a fully automated 3D synapse pipeline: Faster R-CNN detection, z-continuity to drop false positives, and Dijkstra plus GrabCut to segment synaptic clefts.
ocar.resolution: Validated against manual tracking, they report average detection precision of 92.8% (anisotropic) and 93.5% (isotropic) and segmentation precision of 88.6% and 93.0%, presented as state-of-the-art on those EM volumes.
ocar.future_work: They frame the method as giving neurologists a rapid way to obtain synaptic statistics; generalization beyond the tested anisotropic and isotropic volumes is the open question.

summaries.beginner: Finding every synapse in electron-microscope images is slow if people do it by hand. This paper describes a fully automatic computer pipeline that finds synapses and outlines their gaps in 3D.
summaries.intermediate: In BMC Bioinformatics (2018), Xiao, Li, Deng, Chen, Yang, Xie and Han detect synapses with Faster R-CNN, suppress false positives using z-continuity, and segment clefts with Dijkstra and GrabCut. On anisotropic and isotropic EM volumes they report detection precision of 92.8% and 93.5% and segmentation precision of 88.6% and 93.0%, with manual validation. Catalog tags include segmentation, synapses, and electron microscopy.
summaries.advanced: The quoted percentages are average precision as stated in the abstract, not a full precision–recall curve. Dataset identity, synapse count, and comparison methods are not named here. ‘State-of-the-art’ is the authors’ summary of those two volume classes.

plain_language_summary: Finding every synapse in electron-microscope images is slow if people do it by hand. This paper describes a fully automatic computer pipeline that finds synapses and outlines their gaps in 3D.

ocar.opportunity: Hub neurons that form a rich-club are a conserved network motif. Mouse work had tied hubs to coupled expression of metabolism genes; C. elegans, with a nearly complete neuronal connectome and gene-expression atlas, can test whether hub pairs also share expression.
ocar.challenge: Any hub–hub expression similarity might be explained by cell class, distance, transmitter, birth time, lineage, or module membership rather than hub identity itself.
ocar.action: Arnatkevičiūtė, Fornito and colleagues, in PLoS Computational Biology (2018), combined chemical and electrical connectivity of 279 C. elegans neurons with binary expression of 948 genes, scoring correlated expression for every pair.
ocar.resolution: Hub–hub connections were the most similar in expression and nonhub–nonhub the least. Genes contributing most involved glutamatergic and cholinergic signaling and other communication processes. The coupling was not explained by the listed confounders and instead tracked the identity of most hubs as command interneurons that regulate locomotion.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest a conserved transcriptional signature of hubs related to higher-order behaviors, inviting tests in other species and scales.

summaries.beginner: Some worm neurons have far more connections than others and talk among themselves. This study finds that those well-connected cells also tend to turn on similar sets of genes, especially ones used for chemical signaling and for controlling crawling.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2018), Arnatkevičiūtė, Fulcher, Pocock and Fornito scored gene-expression similarity across 279 C. elegans neurons (948 genes) against chemical and electrical connectivity. Hub–hub synapses were the most transcriptionally similar. Controls for subtype, distance, neurotransmitter, birth time, lineage, and module failed to explain the effect, which instead aligned with command-interneuron identity. Catalog tags include elegans, network motifs, graph analysis, and the White+ dataset.
summaries.advanced: Expression is binary across 948 genes, not quantitative RNA-seq. ‘Hub’ and ‘rich-club’ definitions are not restated numerically in the abstract. The locomotion-related interpretation is correlative: command-interneuron identity is the remaining associated factor after the listed controls.

plain_language_summary: Some worm neurons have far more connections than others and talk among themselves. This study finds that those well-connected cells also tend to turn on similar sets of genes, especially ones used for chemical signaling and for controlling crawling.

ocar.opportunity: Hugin neurons in Drosophila regulate feeding and locomotion analogously to mammalian neuromedinU. An EM reconstruction of the larval CNS can show whether those cells also use fast synaptic transmission and how they sit between chemosensation and endocrine outputs.
ocar.challenge: Peptidergic cells are often treated as modulators only, leaving their synaptic partners and co-transmitters unclear.
ocar.action: Schlegel, Texada and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2016), reconstructed the entire connectome of hugin-producing neurons in the Drosophila larval CNS and combined that map with functional tests of peptide and acetylcholine.
ocar.resolution: Hugin neurons use synaptic transmission in addition to peptidergic neuromodulation; acetylcholine is a key transmitter, and both hugin peptide and acetylcholine are required for the feeding effect. Subtypes connect chemosensory to endocrine systems by mixed synaptic and peptide-receptor routes, including DH44 (CRH-like) and insulin-like peptide cells—parallels to neuromedinU downstream targets in mammals.
ocar.future_work: They propose hugin neurons as part of a physiological control system conserved at functional, molecular, and network-architecture levels, inviting comparative tests of that conservation.

summaries.beginner: Some brain cells control eating using slow chemical messengers. This larval-fly study maps those cells’ wiring and shows they also use a fast chemical, acetylcholine, and sit between taste sensors and hormone-releasing cells.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2016), Schlegel, Texada, Miroschnikow, Schoofs, Hückesfeld and colleagues reconstruct the full connectome of Drosophila larval hugin neurons from EM. They show synaptic plus peptidergic transmission, identify acetylcholine as a key co-transmitter, and find both peptide and acetylcholine necessary for feeding regulation. Subtypes bridge chemosensory inputs to endocrine neurons including DH44 and insulin-like peptide cells. Catalog tags include fly and DS03 Drosophila larva.
summaries.advanced: ‘Entire connectome of hugin-producing neurons’ is the authors’ reconstruction claim; completeness metrics are not in the abstract. Conservation with mammalian neuromedinU is analogical (peptide homology and downstream peptide families), not a demonstration of identical circuit motifs. Dual necessity of peptide and acetylcholine is stated without effect sizes here.

plain_language_summary: Some brain cells control eating using slow chemical messengers. This larval-fly study maps those cells’ wiring and shows they also use a fast chemical, acetylcholine, and sit between taste sensors and hormone-releasing cells.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM connectomics samples the depth axis by physically cutting sections, so correcting axial spacing from images alone would salvage distorted volumes without extra hardware.
ocar.challenge: Sectioning has limited precision, producing inhomogeneous non-planar axial sampling. Series may even be collected and imaged in unknown order.
ocar.action: Hanslovsky, Bogovic and Saalfeld, in Bioinformatics (2015), developed image-based methods to identify and correct continuous and discontinuous non-planar axial distortion, including section order, without additional physical measurements.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate the methods in proof-of-principle experiments and real-world problems, and release Fiji libraries plus Spark-capable code for high-performance environments.
ocar.future_work: Open implementations (section-sort, z-spacing, z-spacing-spark) invite application to further serial-section series where physical z-measurements are unavailable.

summaries.beginner: When a brain sample is sliced for the microscope, slices can be uneven, warped, or even stacked in the wrong order. This paper shows how to detect and fix those depth errors using only the images themselves.
summaries.intermediate: In Bioinformatics (2015), Hanslovsky, Bogovic and Saalfeld address axial distortion in serial-section microscopy, including unknown section order. Their image-based corrections require no extra physical apparatus. They report proof-of-principle and real-world tests and ship Fiji plus Spark implementations. Catalog stages include preparation, sectioning, graph analysis, and electron microscopy as method.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not quantify residual z-error or name the real-world volumes. ‘Non-planar’ distortion includes both continuous spacing errors and discontinuous order errors; performance may differ between those regimes. Methods assume image content is informative about adjacency, which can fail in textureless or highly damaged sections.

plain_language_summary: When a brain sample is sliced for the microscope, slices can be uneven, warped, or even stacked in the wrong order. This paper shows how to detect and fix those depth errors using only the images themselves.

ocar.opportunity: Fully automated detection of chemical synapses in highly anisotropic ssTEM would remove the need for a prior cell segmentation and for a fully annotated training subvolume.
ocar.challenge: Anisotropic axial versus lateral resolution makes 3D synapse cues hard. Many methods need dense labels or a prior neuron segmentation.
ocar.action: Kreshuk, Hamprecht and colleagues, in PLoS ONE (2014), classify pixels with 3D features, segment with an Ising MRF, then classify objects, training on sparse user labels in ilastik/vigra.
ocar.resolution: On 238 synapses in 20 serial mouse visual-cortex images (7197×7351 pixels, 4.5×4.5×45 nm), labeled by three annotators and an expert, they report 12% false negatives and 7% false positives, better than then-state-of-the-art without requiring prior cell segmentation. Software and gold standard are released.
ocar.future_work: The public ilastik workflow is meant to be reused on other anisotropic ssTEM synapse-detection problems.

summaries.beginner: Chemical contacts between brain cells can be spotted automatically in a stack of electron-microscope slices, even when the slices are much thicker than the pixels are wide. This paper trains a computer on a few human marks rather than a fully painted volume.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2014), Kreshuk, Köthe, Pax, Bock and Hamprecht detect chemical synapses in anisotropic ssTEM via 3D pixel features, an Ising MRF, and object-level classification from sparse labels. Validation used 238 synapses in 20 mouse visual-cortex sections at 4.5×4.5×45 nm, with three annotators plus expert review. Errors were 12% false negative and 7% false positive, without prior cell segmentation. Code and data are at ilastik.org. Catalog tags include mouse, ssTEM, ilastik, sectioning, acquisition, segmentation, and proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Error rates are on this 20-section mouse visual-cortex set; three-annotator gold standard still required expert re-verification. ‘Better than state-of-the-art’ is claimed for a comparison that is not named in the abstract. The method targets chemical synapses in highly anisotropic TEM, not isotropic FIB-SEM.

plain_language_summary: Chemical contacts between brain cells can be spotted automatically in a stack of electron-microscope slices, even when the slices are much thicker than the pixels are wide. This paper trains a computer on a few human marks rather than a fully painted volume.

ocar.opportunity: Every nervous system is under neuromodulation delivered as local hormones, cotransmitters, or circulating substances. Understanding circuits requires treating modulators as the agents that build functional networks on an anatomical skeleton.
ocar.challenge: An anatomical connectome lists a minimal structure; it does not specify which functional circuits are assembled at a given time because modulators transform intrinsic firing and effective synaptic strength.
ocar.action: Marder, in Neuron (2012), reviews how neuromodulatory substances reconfigure neuronal circuits and often massively alter their output.
ocar.resolution: The essay’s resolution is conceptual: the anatomical connectome is a minimal structure, and the neuromodulatory environment constructs and specifies the functional circuits that give rise to behavior.
ocar.future_work: The implied research program is to restore neuromodulatory state as a first-class variable when interpreting connectomes and predicting behavior.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring is only a starting sketch: chemical modulators can retune cells and connections so the same diagram produces different behaviors. This review explains why those chemicals have to be part of any story about how circuits work.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2012), Eve Marder reviews neuromodulation of neuronal circuits. Modulators arrive as local hormones, cotransmitters in projection neurons, or via the circulation, changing intrinsic firing and effective synaptic strength. Because they reconfigure circuits, she argues the anatomical connectome is a minimal structure and the neuromodulatory environment specifies functional circuits for behavior. The piece is a perspective, not a new empirical map.
summaries.advanced: No new dataset or quantitative reconfiguration example is reported in the abstract. The ‘minimal structure’ claim is a framing of stomatogastric and related work, not a proof that anatomy is uninformative. Electrical synapses and extrasynaptic transmission are not separately treated here.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring is only a starting sketch: chemical modulators can retune cells and connections so the same diagram produces different behaviors. This review explains why those chemicals have to be part of any story about how circuits work.

ocar.opportunity: A synapse-resolution connectome of the mammalian inner plexiform layer, combined with molecular and activity markers, could reveal network motifs that light microscopy cannot.
ocar.challenge: Adjacency without synaptic contact is abundant in retina, so geometry at light- or low-resolution EM cannot reliably map connections; synapses and gap junctions must be seen directly.
ocar.action: Anderson, Jones and colleagues, in Molecular Vision (2011), assembled the 16.5-terabyte rabbit retinal connectome RC1 (≈2 nm, 0.25 mm column) with automated TEM, mosaicking, and registration, plus markers for GABA, glutamate, glycine, taurine, glutamine, and an in vivo activity marker, explored in Viking.
ocar.resolution: They recapitulate known connections and report new features: AII pathways with no fewer than 17 signaling modes; bipolar-cell axons as integration compartments with axonal veto synapses; common conventional-synapse chains including glycinergic–GABAergic crossover; molecular/excitation mapping that splits ultrastructural bipolar groups. They conclude TEM connectomics is practical for network discovery.
ocar.future_work: Surveys of RC1 imply further motif discovery in AII and amacrine chains, and they warn against inferring synapses from process geometry alone in future maps.

summaries.beginner: This team built a very detailed 3D map of a column of rabbit retina, tagging chemical identities of cells as well as their contacts. They show that many connections cannot be guessed from cell shape alone and that well-known pathways are more elaborate than textbooks listed.
summaries.intermediate: In Molecular Vision (2011), Anderson, Jones, Watt and colleagues describe retinal connectome RC1: 16.5 TB of rabbit inner retina at ≈2 nm over a 0.25 mm column, with amino-acid and activity markers, annotated in Viking. Findings include ≥17 AII signaling modes, axonal bipolar synapses and veto inputs, intercalated glycine–GABA chains, and molecular segregation of bipolar groups. They argue only direct visualization of synapses and gap junctions suffices. Catalog tags include mouse-retina dataset labels, TEM, acquisition, alignment, proofreading, infrastructure, and graph analysis; the tissue in the abstract is rabbit.
summaries.advanced: The catalog organism/dataset fields say mouse retina while the paper’s RC1 volume is rabbit; pedagogy should follow the abstract. ‘No less than 17’ AII modes and 16.5 TB / 0.25 mm / ≈2 nm are the authors’ figures. Long amacrine chains and ON–OFF crossover are anatomical interpretations supporting prior physiology, not new recordings.

plain_language_summary: This team built a very detailed 3D map of a column of rabbit retina, tagging chemical identities of cells as well as their contacts. They show that many connections cannot be guessed from cell shape alone and that well-known pathways are more elaborate than textbooks listed.

ocar.opportunity: Tiled ssTEM of large brains, especially larval Drosophila, needs automatic registration that recovers 3D continuity despite sectioning, staining, and imaging distortions.
ocar.challenge: Tiles must be placed despite staining artifacts, mechanical deformation, missing sections, and dissimilarity of structures across consecutive sections.
ocar.action: Saalfeld, Cardona, Hartenstein and Tomancak, in Bioinformatics (2010), developed a fully automatic as-rigid-as-possible method using SIFT landmarks within and across sections and a global least-squares pose of all tiles, implemented in TrakEM2/Fiji.
ocar.resolution: They evaluate precision on an artificial TEM-like dataset and register a first-instar Drosophila larval brain ssTEM set of 6885 images.
ocar.future_work: The open TrakEM2 implementation is the vehicle for applying the same non-rigid mosaicking to other large ssTEM series.

summaries.beginner: Large electron-microscope mosaics are made of many overlapping tiles that have been stretched and stained unevenly. This paper automatically finds matching landmarks and gently warps the tiles so a fly larva’s brain stack lines up in 3D.
summaries.intermediate: In Bioinformatics (2010), Saalfeld, Cardona, Hartenstein and Tomancak register large tiled ssTEM with SIFT correspondences and global least-squares, remaining as rigid as possible. They test on synthetic TEM-like data and on 6885 images of the first-instar Drosophila larval brain. The method ships in TrakEM2 via Fiji. Catalog tags include fly, ssTEM, TrakEM2, DS03 Drosophila larva, preparation, sectioning, acquisition, and alignment.
summaries.advanced: The 6885-image larval brain is the scale demonstration; residual error on that volume is not numeric in the abstract. ‘As-rigid-as-possible’ still permits non-rigid correction of section distortion. Missing sections and strong appearance change across sections remain failure modes the method is designed to tolerate, not eliminate.

plain_language_summary: Large electron-microscope mosaics are made of many overlapping tiles that have been stretched and stained unevenly. This paper automatically finds matching landmarks and gently warps the tiles so a fly larva’s brain stack lines up in 3D.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes more complex than C. elegans require computers to segment neural shapes so synapses at contacts can be checked. New metrics and machine learning that minimize those metrics have sharply reduced computer errors.
ocar.challenge: Image segmentation is laborious for humans. Without proper metrics, one cannot even quantify how a computer disagrees with true segmentations.
ocar.action: Jain, Seung and Turaga, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2010), review new performance metrics for segmentation and learning methods that search for algorithms minimizing those metrics.
ocar.resolution: They argue errors have fallen enough that correcting remaining mistakes should now be faster than segmenting by hand, a crucial step toward connectomes beyond C. elegans.
ocar.future_work: They expect further reductions in human effort, which they treat as essential for reconstructing more complex connectomes.

summaries.beginner: To map brain wiring, computers must outline cells in microscope images, and people then fix the leftover mistakes. This review says the computers have improved enough that fixing their errors should beat tracing everything by hand.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2010), Jain, Seung and Turaga review machine learning for image segmentation in connectomics. They emphasize metrics that quantify disagreement with true segmentations and learners that minimize those metrics. Reduced error rates, they argue, make human correction faster than de novo manual segmentation—necessary for connectomes more complex than C. elegans. Catalog tags include elegans, DS01 White+, and segmentation.
summaries.advanced: No numeric error rates appear in the abstract. The C. elegans comparison is a complexity horizon, not a claim that nematode segmentation is solved. The review predates later flood-filling and transformer methods; remaining-error arguments are of their time.

plain_language_summary: To map brain wiring, computers must outline cells in microscope images, and people then fix the leftover mistakes. This review says the computers have improved enough that fixing their errors should beat tracing everything by hand.

ocar.opportunity: A connection matrix of the human brain would be an indispensable foundation for basic and applied neurobiology, analogous to collated large-scale connection patterns in other mammals.
ocar.challenge: The network of anatomical connections among human neuronal elements was still largely unknown, with no human connection matrix and no coordinated effort to collect, archive, and disseminate one.
ocar.action: Sporns, Tononi and Kötter, in PLoS Computational Biology (2005), propose a research strategy to build the human ‘connectome’ and discuss its potential impact.
ocar.resolution: The paper names the problem and a program: treat the human connection matrix as a community data goal rather than an incidental byproduct of individual tracing studies.
ocar.future_work: The strategy they outline is the future work—collecting, archiving, and sharing human anatomical connection data in a coordinated way.

summaries.beginner: In 2005, researchers argued that the human brain’s wiring diagram should be treated as a shared map the field must collect on purpose. At the time no such matrix existed, unlike some maps for other mammals.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2005), Sporns, Tononi and Kötter introduce the human ‘connectome’ as the connection matrix of the human brain. They note that while large-scale anatomical collations exist for other mammals, no human matrix or coordinated collection effort existed. The paper proposes a research strategy and discusses impact. Catalog tags include infrastructure. This is a founding perspective, not an empirical human EM volume.
summaries.advanced: ‘Connectome’ here is a structural connection matrix at a scale left open in the abstract (not synapse-resolution EM). No dataset is released. Impact arguments are prospective as of 2005.

plain_language_summary: In 2005, researchers argued that the human brain’s wiring diagram should be treated as a shared map the field must collect on purpose. At the time no such matrix existed, unlike some maps for other mammals.

ocar.opportunity: Bristle mechanosensory neurons around the Drosophila head are somatotopically organized and drive aimed grooming. A full adult fly brain ssEM reconstruction can list nearly all of their synaptic partners.
ocar.challenge: How mechanosensory neurons interface with brain circuits to turn touch location into location-appropriate grooming was unclear.
ocar.action: Calle-Schuler, Seeds and colleagues, in eLife (2026), used a serial-section EM reconstruction of a full adult fly brain to identify nearly all pre- and postsynaptic partners of head bristle mechanosensory neurons.
ocar.resolution: Postsynaptic partners dominate and include excitatory and inhibitory cells. An excitatory cholinergic hemilineage (23b) elicits aimed head grooming and connects differentially with bristles from distinct head locations—a lineage-based parallel somatotopic architecture. Presynaptic partners provide extensive BMN presynaptic inhibition, consistent with sensory gain control for suppressing movements and sequencing grooming.
ocar.future_work: They present this as the first comprehensive somatotopic connectome of its kind and a template for how feedforward excitation/inhibition, feedback inhibition, and developmental lineage shape mechanosensory processing.

summaries.beginner: When something touches a fly’s head, the fly grooms the right spot. This paper maps the brain cells that receive those touch signals and shows they are arranged by location on the head, with both ‘go’ and ‘stop’ connections.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2026), Calle-Schuler, Santana-Cruz, Kmecova, Hampel and Seeds reconstruct nearly all partners of Drosophila head bristle mechanosensory neurons in a full adult brain ssEM volume (catalog DS04 FAFB). Postsynaptic partners dominate; hemilineage 23b is a cholinergic excitatory path for aimed head grooming with location-specific BMN connectivity. Presynaptic inhibition onto BMNs fits gain-control models of grooming sequence. Catalog stages include sectioning and synapses.
summaries.advanced: ‘Nearly all’ partners is the authors’ completeness language; residual missed synapses are not quantified here. Functional roles of hemilineage 23b and gain control are tied to this connectome plus prior grooming work (Eichler et al., 2024, cited in the abstract), not fully re-derived from anatomy alone. FAFB is one brain; stereotypy across individuals is not measured in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When something touches a fly’s head, the fly grooms the right spot. This paper maps the brain cells that receive those touch signals and shows they are arranged by location on the head, with both ‘go’ and ‘stop’ connections.

ocar.opportunity: Modern EM connectomes can classify postsynaptic targets (soma, shaft, spine) at circuit scale if a cheap method exists that uses only neuron meshes, not images.
ocar.challenge: Accurate spine and component classification across entire volumes has been hard at connectome scale because image-based methods are costly.
ocar.action: Pedigo, Collman and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), built a mesh-geometry pipeline with cloud optimizations, trained a simple classifier on MICrONS, and applied it to more than 207.3 million synapses, also testing H01 without retraining.
ocar.resolution: Weighted F1 was 0.961 on MICrONS and 0.949 on H01. The census recovers expected excitatory-to-spine targeting and exceptions (L5 near-projecting and L6 corticothalamic cells often targeting excitatory shafts), plus variable multi-innervated spines even within a type. Predictions, code, and cloud deployment are released; they quote a few hundred dollars in cloud cost for hundreds of thousands of neurons.
ocar.future_work: They argue mesh-derived features can be a general primitive for morphologies in future reconstructions beyond MICrONS and H01.

summaries.beginner: Brain maps now include millions of contacts, but each contact lands on a different part of the receiving cell. This preprint trains a cheap computer method, using only the cell’s 3D surface, to say whether a contact hits a spine, a shaft, or the cell body.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Pedigo, Danskin, Dorkenwald, da Costa, Schneider-Mizell, Collman and colleagues classify postsynaptic structures from neuron meshes alone. A MICrONS-trained classifier reaches weighted F1 0.961 and maps over 207.3 million synapses; on H01 human cortex without retraining, F1 is 0.949. They report expected spine targeting plus exceptions in L5 NP and L6 CT cells, and variable multi-synapse spines. Catalog organisms include mouse and human; datasets DS13 MICrONS and DS14 H01.
summaries.advanced: F1 scores are weighted figures from the abstract; class-wise errors are not given. ‘Few hundred dollars’ is their cloud-cost claim. H01 generalization without retraining is encouraging but still two mammalian cortical volumes. Multi-innervated-spine frequency is described as surprising variability, not a causal claim.

plain_language_summary: Brain maps now include millions of contacts, but each contact lands on a different part of the receiving cell. This preprint trains a cheap computer method, using only the cell’s 3D surface, to say whether a contact hits a spine, a shaft, or the cell body.

ocar.opportunity: Combining high-resolution EM with advanced light microscopy has yielded complete fly connectomes and dynamic activity profiles in mice and zebrafish, promising to link static anatomy to physiology and to disease.
ocar.challenge: Managing terabyte-to-petabyte datasets, improving spatiotemporal resolution, fusing modalities, and handling ethical issues remain open. Translating synaptic maps to clinical neuroscience is still early.
ocar.action: Ahmed, Tang and colleagues, in New Medicine (2026), review core connectomics methods: imaging, tissue preparation, computational reconstruction, and multimodal fusion, with emphasis on correlating anatomy with physiological events.
ocar.resolution: The review surveys breakthroughs including complete Drosophila connectomes and activity profiles in mouse and zebrafish, and discusses translational mapping of synaptic alterations in ASD and Alzheimer’s disease.
ocar.future_work: They highlight remaining challenges in scale, resolution, ethics, and clinical translation as the agenda after current multimodal pipelines.

summaries.beginner: This review explains how light and electron microscopes are being combined to map brain wiring at many scales. It also discusses why the resulting data are huge, how they might relate to disease, and what problems still stand in the way.
summaries.intermediate: In New Medicine (2026), Ahmed, Zhang, Yue and colleagues review brain connectomics spanning nanoscale synapses to mesoscale networks. They cover imaging, preparation, reconstruction, and light–EM fusion, citing complete Drosophila connectomes and dynamic profiles in mice and zebrafish. Challenges include terabyte–petabyte management, spatiotemporal resolution, and ethics. Translational sections address synaptic alterations in ASD and Alzheimer’s. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, graph analysis, and a zebrafish dataset label.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a primary multimodal volume. Disease applications (ASD, AD) are exploratory in the abstract. Catalog organism/dataset (fly, DS15 zebrafish) should not be read as the paper’s single experimental system.

plain_language_summary: This review explains how light and electron microscopes are being combined to map brain wiring at many scales. It also discusses why the resulting data are huge, how they might relate to disease, and what problems still stand in the way.

ocar.opportunity: The human fovea packs more than 50 neuron types whose synaptic interconnections have been hard to determine. An AI-assisted, proofreadable first-draft connectome of a foveal sample could be shared worldwide.
ocar.challenge: How these densely packed types interconnect to transmit visual information, including circuits for color vision, remained difficult to map in human tissue.
ocar.action: Kim, Packer, Macrina, Lee and colleagues, in PNAS (2026), used AI-based computational methods to create a first-draft wiring diagram of every neuron and synapse in a sample of human fovea.
ocar.resolution: They report a freely available connectomic resource and, so far, synaptic circuits linked to human color vision as an example of what makes human retinal wiring distinctive.
ocar.future_work: As a first draft, the resource is meant for community proofreading and further circuit discovery in the human fovea.

summaries.beginner: The tiny center of human vision contains many specialized cell types whose connections were largely unknown. This paper releases a first computer-assisted wiring map of a piece of that tissue, including circuits used for color vision.
summaries.intermediate: In Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2026), Kim, Packer, Macrina, Pollreisz, Curcio, Lee, Kemnitz and colleagues present an AI-based first-draft connectome of a human foveal sample, intended to be proofreadable and public. They highlight synaptic circuits linked to human color vision. Catalog stages include proofreading and graph analysis; catalog organism/dataset fields list mouse retina, while the abstract is human fovea.
summaries.advanced: ‘Every neuron and synapse’ is the authors’ description of the sample, not a whole-fovea census. Color-vision circuits are ‘discoveries so far.’ Catalog metadata (mouse, DS09/DS10) conflict with the human fovea abstract and should not override the paper’s stated tissue.

plain_language_summary: The tiny center of human vision contains many specialized cell types whose connections were largely unknown. This paper releases a first computer-assisted wiring map of a piece of that tissue, including circuits used for color vision.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila VNC connectomes make it possible to simulate which cells and synapses could generate walking rhythms, a CPG whose structure was not known in any animal.
ocar.challenge: Central pattern generators produce oscillations without oscillating input, but identifying a minimal walking CPG among VNC neurons is non-trivial.
ocar.action: Pugliese, Tuthill, Brunton and colleagues, on bioRxiv (catalog year 2026), built dynamic simulations of Drosophila VNC connectomes, screened descending neurons, pruned to a minimal rhythm-generating circuit, and tested a predicted second descending path with optogenetics in behaving flies.
ocar.resolution: DNg100, a known walking command neuron, was the top driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. A three-neuron motif (one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons) was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations predicted DNb08 also drives rhythmic leg movements, confirmed optogenetically.
ocar.future_work: They present cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative walking CPG; further physiology can test how this motif interacts with other locomotor modules.

summaries.beginner: Walking depends on brain circuits that can beat out a rhythm even without a rhythmic input. Using fly nerve-cord wiring diagrams, this preprint finds a small set of cells that can generate leg rhythms and checks a prediction in real flies.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (catalogued 2026), Pugliese, Chou, Abe, Turcu, Lancaster, Tuthill and Brunton simulate Drosophila VNC connectomes (catalog DS07 FANC/MANC). A descending-neuron activation screen ranks DNg100 as the top driver of rhythmic leg motor output. Network pruning isolates a three-neuron CPG (one inhibitory, two excitatory interneurons) necessary and sufficient across all six legs and four connectomes. A separate descending path, DNb08, is predicted and confirmed with optogenetics in behaving flies.
summaries.advanced: ‘Necessary and sufficient’ is a simulation result on connectome dynamics plus one optogenetic confirmation (DNb08), not a full in vivo lesion of the three interneurons. Four connectome datasets are claimed; names beyond catalog FANC/MANC are not listed in the abstract. Cellular parameters (gains, time constants) used in simulation are not specified here.

plain_language_summary: Walking depends on brain circuits that can beat out a rhythm even without a rhythmic input. Using fly nerve-cord wiring diagrams, this preprint finds a small set of cells that can generate leg rhythms and checks a prediction in real flies.

ocar.opportunity: Prior retinal EM volumes were too small for rare types and large dendritic arbors. A ~1 mm² adult mouse retina EM dataset with functional imaging and community proofreading could become a shared cell-type and wiring resource.
ocar.challenge: Limited volume size blocked mosaics of rare types. High-throughput cell typing and mixed ribbon versus conventional synapse detection remain unfinished at this scale.
ocar.action: Ströh, Ebert and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), describe Eyewire II, an EM volume covering nearly 1 mm² of adult mouse retina—about 10–100 times larger than previous retinal EM volumes—with two-photon Ca²⁺ imaging in a subset of cells, automated reconstruction, and human-in-the-loop typing.
ocar.resolution: Proofreading so far yielded more than 8,000 bipolar, 13,000 amacrine, and 4,000 retinal ganglion cells; ribbon detection is complete and conventional synapses are in progress. Morphological features recover all 15 known bipolar types as regular mosaics. More than 30 laboratories are contributing.
ocar.future_work: The resource is advancing toward a complete cell-type catalog and synaptic wiring diagram of a mammalian retina.

summaries.beginner: This project images a much larger patch of mouse retina than earlier wiring studies and invites many labs to help finish the cell list. Some cells were also recorded while they saw movies, so shape and function can be lined up.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Ströh, Ebert, Fadjukov and colleagues introduce Eyewire II: nearly 1 mm² of adult mouse retina EM, roughly 10–100× prior retinal EM volumes, with two-photon calcium imaging of visual responses including natural movies. Human proofreading of automated reconstruction has so far produced >8,000 bipolar, >13,000 amacrine, and >4,000 ganglion cells. A human-in-the-loop classifier recovers all 15 known bipolar types as non-overlapping mosaics. Catalog tags include mouse, EyeWire, two-photon, EM, alignment, proofreading, graph analysis, and DS09/DS10.
summaries.advanced: Cell counts are ‘so far’ and synapse detection is incomplete for conventional synapses. ‘All 15 known bipolar types’ is a proof-of-principle on morphology, not a finished catalog of amacrine or RGC types. Volume size comparisons (10–100×) are the authors’ relative scale.

plain_language_summary: This project images a much larger patch of mouse retina than earlier wiring studies and invites many labs to help finish the cell list. Some cells were also recorded while they saw movies, so shape and function can be lined up.

ocar.opportunity: Multiple Drosophila brain and VNC connectomes exist, but comparing them requires cell typing. An automatic alignment from network topology alone could assign types in a female VNC using male references and find sex differences.
ocar.challenge: Existing cell typing typically needs extensive manual curation. Sex-specific and sexually dimorphic types are easy to miss without a systematic comparison.
ocar.action: Matsliah, Salmon, Bates and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), automatically align connectomes via network topology and use two complete male VNC connectomes as references to type intrinsic neurons of the female VNC.
ocar.resolution: They assign cell types to about 13,000 neurons intrinsic to the female VNC, automatically identify sex-specific and sexually dimorphic types, and compare circuits for male song production and female oviposition with their counterparts in the other sex.
ocar.future_work: They present the methods as a path to comparative connectomics at scale for circuits linking brain and body.

summaries.beginner: Male and female flies have similar nerve cords but not identical wiring. This preprint matches cells across sexes using only connection patterns, then points to circuits used for singing in males and egg-laying in females.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Matsliah, Salmon, Bates, Yang, Lee, Saul, Silverman and colleagues align Drosophila VNCs from topology alone. Using two complete male VNCs as references, they type ~13,000 intrinsic neurons in the female VNC and flag sex-specific and sexually dimorphic types. They focus on song-production versus oviposition circuits and their cross-sex counterparts. Catalog tags include fly, alignment, graph analysis, and DS07 VNC (FANC/MANC).
summaries.advanced: Type assignment is automatic from topology; the abstract does not report a numeric accuracy against a fully curated female atlas. ‘~13,000’ is their count of intrinsic female VNC neurons typed. Functional interpretations of song and oviposition differences follow from connectivity plus known behaviors, not new physiology in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Male and female flies have similar nerve cords but not identical wiring. This preprint matches cells across sexes using only connection patterns, then points to circuits used for singing in males and egg-laying in females.

ocar.opportunity: A fly visual-projection-neuron connectome makes it possible to census mitochondria shape and position relative to synapses across many cell types, searching for systematic cell-biological rules.
ocar.challenge: Little was known about how mitochondria are organized within the circuits of a whole connectome, despite their roles in calcium handling and energy production.
ocar.action: Sager, Pfeiffer and colleagues, in Science (2025), analyzed morphological and spatial organization of more than 100,000 mitochondria in over 1,000 Drosophila visual projection neurons.
ocar.resolution: Mitochondrial shape and size differ systematically by cell type, enough to serve as an identifying fingerprint. They derive three positioning rules: precision of 2–3 microns; different pre- versus postsynaptic preferences in axons versus dendrites; and cell-type specialization correlated with visual responses and input connectivity. In olfactory learning circuits, mitochondria are enriched at presynapses onto particular partners by accumulating in axonal subcompartments.
ocar.future_work: These organizing principles add cell-biological dimensions for interpreting circuit function in connectomes more generally.

summaries.beginner: Energy-producing mitochondria inside nerve cells are not scattered at random. Mapping them across many fly visual cells, this paper finds that each cell type has a recognizable mitochondrial layout, placed with micrometre-scale care near specific connections.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2025), Sager, Pfeiffer, Wu and colleagues quantify more than 100,000 mitochondria in over 1,000 Drosophila visual projection neurons. Shape and size distinguish cell types. Positioning follows three rules: 2–3 µm precision; axon/dendrite-specific preference for pre- versus postsynaptic sites; and type-specific placement that correlates with visual responses and connectivity. In mushroom-body-related olfactory learning circuitry, mitochondria enrich at selected presynapses via axonal subcompartments. Catalog dataset field lists DS13 MICrONS while the abstract is fly visual neurons.
summaries.advanced: The 2–3 micron precision and ‘>100,000’ / ‘>1,000’ counts are from the abstract. Fingerprint-level discriminability is claimed without a classifier accuracy number here. Catalog MICrONS tagging conflicts with the Drosophila visual-projection-neuron system in the text. Correlations with visual responses do not prove mitochondria cause those responses.

plain_language_summary: Energy-producing mitochondria inside nerve cells are not scattered at random. Mapping them across many fly visual cells, this paper finds that each cell type has a recognizable mitochondrial layout, placed with micrometre-scale care near specific connections.

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila central brain connectome, with more than 125,000 neurons and 50 million synaptic connections, is a template for asking whether connectivity plus transmitter identity can predict whole-brain sensorimotor transformations.
ocar.challenge: Feeding and grooming depend on distributed circuits; it is unclear whether a leaky integrate-and-fire model with no extra fitted physiology can predict which neurons respond, which are required, and how taste modalities interact.
ocar.action: Shiu, Sterne and colleagues, in Nature (2024), built a leaky integrate-and-fire model of the entire Drosophila brain from connectivity and neurotransmitter identity, then computationally activated gustatory and mechanosensory neurons and tested predictions with optogenetics and behavior.
ocar.resolution: Sugar- or water-sensing activation predicted taste-responsive neurons required for feeding initiation. Activating feeding-region neurons predicted motor-neuron firing, validated optogenetically. Taste-class activations predicted aversive versus appetitive interactions. Mechanosensory activation predicted the antennal grooming circuit and subtype responses.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the model as a generator of testable hypotheses for complete sensorimotor transformations from synapse-level connectivity and predicted transmitters alone.

summaries.beginner: With a wiring diagram of the fruit-fly brain, researchers built a computer model that lets virtual taste or touch cells fire. The model guessed which other cells should respond and which movements should follow, and many of those guesses matched real experiments.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Shiu, Sterne, Spiller and colleagues simulate the adult Drosophila central brain (>125,000 neurons, 50 million synapses) as leaky integrate-and-fire units using connectivity and neurotransmitter identity. Computational activation of sugar- or water-sensing neurons predicted cells that respond to tastes and are required for feeding initiation; feeding-region activations predicted motor firing, confirmed optogenetically. The same framework captured taste-modality interactions and antennal grooming. Catalog stage is modeling; organism is fly.
summaries.advanced: Neuron and synapse counts are those stated for the connectome template. Transmitter identity is predicted, not fully measured for every cell. Success on feeding and grooming does not imply the model captures all behaviors or extrasynaptic modulation. Optogenetic validation is cited for selected predictions, not every node the model ranks.

plain_language_summary: With a wiring diagram of the fruit-fly brain, researchers built a computer model that lets virtual taste or touch cells fire. The model guessed which other cells should respond and which movements should follow, and many of those guesses matched real experiments.

ocar.opportunity: Single-cell transcriptomes of neuronal types plus type-level connectomes could reveal a genetic code for who connects to whom, if a model can turn paired expression into a connectivity-like covariance matrix.
ocar.challenge: Deciphering which genetic interactions dictate connections between neuronal types has been formidable; prior spatial connectome models may miss interactions.
ocar.action: Qiao, on bioRxiv (catalog year 2024), proposed a bilinear model inspired by recommendation systems that maps pre- and postsynaptic gene expression into a covariance matrix matched to a connectomic connectivity matrix, tested on C. elegans and mouse retina.
ocar.resolution: On C. elegans electrical synapses the model matched or slightly exceeded a spatial connectome model while capturing all of that model’s genetic interactions plus additional ones. In mouse retina it recapitulated bipolar-to-ganglion connectivity motifs and highlighted cell-adhesion and synapse-formation genes.
ocar.future_work: The author presents the approach as a benchmark for transcriptomic analysis of synaptic connections and a starting point for mechanistic and perturbation studies of circuit assembly.

summaries.beginner: Why certain types of nerve cells connect, and others do not, is written partly in the genes they express. This preprint fits a simple mathematical model that turns those gene lists into a predicted wiring table and checks it in worms and mouse retina.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (catalogued 2024), Mu Qiao trains a bilinear model so that gene-expression covariance of pre- and postsynaptic types matches a connectivity matrix. On C. elegans it performs comparably to, or slightly better than, a spatial connectome model for electrical synapses and infers extra genetic interactions.
