On mouse retina it recovers bipolar–RGC motifs and interpretable adhesion/synapse-formation signatures. Catalog tags include elegans, mouse, graph analysis, DS01, and DS09/DS10.
summaries.advanced: ‘Slightly better’ than SCM is qualitative in the abstract; no numeric AUROC is given. Electrical synapses in C. elegans and bipolar–RGC motifs in retina are distinct tests, not a universal genetic code. Covariance matching is correlative: identified genes are candidates, not proven wiring determinants.

plain_language_summary: Why certain types of nerve cells connect, and others do not, is written partly in the genes they express. This preprint fits a simple mathematical model that turns those gene lists into a predicted wiring table and checks it in worms and mouse retina.

ocar.opportunity: Dense 3D instance segmentation usually needs expensive volumetric ground truth. If sparse 2D labels plus a 3D network pretrained on synthetic data can bootstrap pseudo ground truth, annotation cost could collapse.
ocar.challenge: Accurate 3D models still seem to demand dense expert labels, a bottleneck across electron, expansion, and live-cell microscopy.
ocar.action: Thiyagarajan, Sheridan, Harris and Manor, on bioRxiv (2024), train a 2D network on sparse labels to predict complete boundaries on every section, then a 3D network pretrained on synthetic data infers inter-section connectivity.
ocar.resolution: Across diverse datasets, 3D models trained on these pseudo ground truths reached accuracy comparable to dense expert annotation, with up to a 1,000-fold reduction in human annotation time and about an order-of-magnitude drop in total reconstruction cost even after proofreading.
ocar.future_work: They frame the method as extending 2D foundation models into 3D and democratizing dense training-data generation.

summaries.beginner: Outlining every cell in a 3D microscope stack usually takes a huge amount of expert drawing. This preprint shows that sparse marks on 2D slices can be enough to teach a 3D model, cutting human drawing time dramatically.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024), Thiyagarajan, Sheridan, Harris and Manor bootstrap dense 3D instance segmentations from sparse 2D annotations: a 2D net completes boundaries per section; a synthetically pretrained 3D net links sections. Validated on electron, expansion, and live-cell microscopy, models trained on pseudo labels match dense-expert accuracy, with up to 1,000-fold less annotation time and ~10-fold lower total cost including proofreading. Catalog stages include segmentation, proofreading, and infrastructure.
summaries.advanced: ‘Up to 1,000-fold’ and ‘order of magnitude’ are the authors’ cost claims; dataset-wise scores are not listed in the abstract. Comparability to dense expert annotation is asserted without a named metric here. Success across three microscopy families still depends on the 3D net’s synthetic pretraining and on downstream proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Outlining every cell in a 3D microscope stack usually takes a huge amount of expert drawing. This preprint shows that sparse marks on 2D slices can be enough to teach a 3D model, cutting human drawing time dramatically.

ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide fly functional imaging needs a common anatomical space so dynamics can be compared across labs and aligned to gene expression and connectomes.
ocar.challenge: Registering in vivo functional volumes to ex vivo atlases must absorb differences in modality, microscope, and sample preparation.
ocar.action: Brezovec, Clandinin and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2023), built an in vivo multiphoton Functional Drosophila Atlas (FDA) and a two-step pipeline, BIFROST, to transform functional data into that space and import ex vivo resources such as connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Using genetically labeled cell types as ground truth, they demonstrate registration precision of less than 10 microns across specimens and laboratories, including alignment of in vivo volumes to ultrastructural connectomes.
ocar.future_work: They position BIFROST for quantitative comparison of functional datasets and direct structure–function registration in future experiments.

summaries.beginner: Fly-brain activity movies from different labs are hard to overlay because the images do not share the same coordinate system. This preprint builds a living-brain atlas and a registration method that lines those movies up to within ten microns, including to wiring diagrams.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Brezovec, Berger, Hao, Lin, Ahmed, Pacheco, Thiberge, Murthy and Clandinin introduce the Functional Drosophila Atlas and BIFROST, a two-step registration pipeline from in vivo multiphoton volumes into a common space that can also import connectomes. Genetically labeled cell types yield <10 µm precision across specimens and labs. Catalog tags include fly, preparation, alignment, and a MICrONS dataset label while the abstract is Drosophila.
summaries.advanced: Sub-10 micron precision is the abstract’s ground-truth figure; error distributions are not given. Catalog MICrONS tagging does not match the fly FDA. Registration to connectomes is demonstrated as feasible; residual modality-specific warps are not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Fly-brain activity movies from different labs are hard to overlay because the images do not share the same coordinate system. This preprint builds a living-brain atlas and a registration method that lines those movies up to within ten microns, including to wiring diagrams.

ocar.opportunity: The numerically tractable Drosophila antennal lobe can test whether a widely distributed neuropeptide modulates olfactory processing uniformly.
ocar.challenge: Many neuropeptides are broadly distributed, so it is unclear whether they have the same effect everywhere in a network.
ocar.action: Sizemore, Jonaitis and Dacks, in 2023 work (Nature Communications DOI; catalogued journal bioRxiv), combined connectomics and in vivo physiology to study myoinhibitory peptide (MIP) in the antennal lobe.
ocar.resolution: Despite uniform MIP distribution, olfactory input decreased in some glomeruli and increased in others. Heterogeneous local interneurons are the sole MIP source; non-uniform effects were not explained by those neurons’ intrinsic connectivity or odor responses, but by differential expression of the inhibitory MIP receptor SPR across glomeruli.
ocar.future_work: The finding that a single peptide–receptor pair can still act non-uniformly implies that receptor maps, not peptide maps alone, should guide predictions of neuromodulation elsewhere.

summaries.beginner: A chemical messenger can be sprinkled evenly through a brain region and still push some cells one way and others the opposite way. In the fly’s smell center, that happens because the receiving lock for the messenger is not evenly installed.
summaries.intermediate: In 2023, Sizemore, Jonaitis and Dacks show that myoinhibitory peptide in the Drosophila antennal lobe is uniformly distributed yet decreases olfactory input in some glomeruli while increasing it in others. MIP comes only from a heterogeneous LN ensemble. Connectomic and physiological measures of those LNs did not explain the mosaic; differential SPR receptor expression across glomeruli did. Catalog organism is fly.
summaries.advanced: Uniform peptide versus mosaic receptor is the mechanistic claim; quantitative receptor-level measurements are not numbered in the abstract. ‘Not likely due to LN intrinsic properties’ is the authors’ interpretation of connectivity and odor-evoked responses. Journal field is bioRxiv while the uuid is a Nature Communications DOI.

plain_language_summary: A chemical messenger can be sprinkled evenly through a brain region and still push some cells one way and others the opposite way. In the fly’s smell center, that happens because the receiving lock for the messenger is not evenly installed.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM connectomics can place Alzheimer’s-related molecules in the full local neuronal and glial milieu if those molecules can be seen in the same volume.
ocar.challenge: Relating Aβ and pTau to circuit alterations requires correlative light and electron microscopy at connectomic scale, which has been scarce as a public resource.
ocar.action: Han, Li, Lichtman-associated authors and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2023), present a volumetric CLEM protocol using fluorescent nanobodies to localize Aβ and pTau in a large-scale hippocampal connectomics dataset from the 3xTg AD mouse, with segmented neurons, glia, and synapses.
ocar.resolution: They release a public vCLEM dataset. Proof-of-principle findings include pTau-positive spine-like protrusions at the axon initial segment and changes in synapse number and size near Aβ plaques.
ocar.future_work: The resource is intended to enable collaborative discovery of molecular and structural alterations in AD and other neurodegenerative diseases within large-scale EM data.

summaries.beginner: Alzheimer’s proteins can now be painted onto a 3D electron-microscope map of mouse hippocampus so researchers can see them next to complete local wiring. The team shares that map and notes odd structures near plaques and at the start of some axons.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Han, Li, Wang, Blakely and colleagues localize amyloid-β and hyperphosphorylated Tau with fluorescent nanobodies inside a volumetric CLEM / large-scale EM dataset from 3xTg AD mouse hippocampus. Segmented neurons, glia, and synapses provide ultrastructural context. They report pTau-positive spine-like AIS protrusions and altered synapse number and size near Aβ plaques, and release the dataset. Catalog tags include mouse, electron microscopy, and segmentation.
summaries.advanced: Proof-of-principle localizations should not be read as a full disease-mechanism model. Synapse number/size changes near plaques are stated without effect sizes in the abstract. The 3xTg model is one AD mouse line; human translation is not claimed here.

plain_language_summary: Alzheimer’s proteins can now be painted onto a 3D electron-microscope map of mouse hippocampus so researchers can see them next to complete local wiring. The team shares that map and notes odd structures near plaques and at the start of some axons.

ocar.opportunity: Male Drosophila produce pulse and sine courtship song with the same wings. Cell-type genetics plus a VNC connectome can show how nested premotor circuits generate those distinct patterns.
ocar.challenge: How premotor circuits flexibly generate diverse movement patterns from a shared muscle set is unclear.
ocar.action: Lillvis, Wang, Dickson and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2023), mapped song circuits in the male VNC using cell-type-specific reagents and the connectome, then activated or inhibited each cell type while recording song.
ocar.resolution: The song circuit comprises two nested feed-forward pathways with extensive reciprocal and feedback connections. The larger network produces pulse song (more complex, ancestral); a subset produces sine song (simpler, more recent).
ocar.future_work: They suggest nested organization may be a common motif when evolution layers flexibility onto a basic movement pattern.

summaries.beginner: Male fruit flies sing in two styles using the same wings. This preprint maps the nerve-cord cells for both songs and finds the simpler song is made by a subset of the circuit that makes the more complex song.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Lillvis, Wang, Shiozaki, Xu, Stern and Dickson reconstruct Drosophila male courtship-song circuits in the VNC with genetic reagents and connectomics, then perturb each cell type. Two nested feed-forward pathways with rich recurrence produce pulse versus sine song; pulse uses the larger network, sine a subset. Catalog tags include fly, DS07 VNC (FANC/MANC), and connectomics.
summaries.advanced: Ancestral versus recent song forms are evolutionary interpretations stated in the abstract, not dated phylogenies with numbers here. Behavioral effects of each cell type are asserted without listing which perturbations abolished which song mode. Nested architecture is a hypothesis for other motor systems.

plain_language_summary: Male fruit flies sing in two styles using the same wings. This preprint maps the nerve-cord cells for both songs and finds the simpler song is made by a subset of the circuit that makes the more complex song.

ocar.opportunity: Graph matching can pair homologous neurons across hemispheres in nanoscale connectomes, but prior methods used only ipsilateral subgraphs.
ocar.challenge: Standard matching treats two isolated networks, discarding contralateral edges that may carry correlated pairing information.
ocar.action: Pedigo, Winding, Priebe and Vogelstein, on bioRxiv (2022), modify a state-of-the-art matcher to solve a ‘bisected’ graph matching problem that includes between-hemisphere connections.
ocar.resolution: When contralateral subgraphs are edge-correlated, simulations and real connectomes show improved pairing accuracy versus ipsilateral-only matching.
ocar.future_work: They expect the method to improve neuron pairing across hemispheres and to apply wherever bisected matching arises.

summaries.beginner: Left–right pairs of brain cells can be found by matching connection patterns, but earlier tools ignored the wires that cross the midline. This preprint uses those crossing wires too and pairs cells more accurately when the two sides agree.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2022), Pedigo, Winding, Priebe and Vogelstein extend graph matching to a bisected problem so contralateral as well as ipsilateral edges inform neuron pairing across hemispheres. Simulations and real connectomes show accuracy gains when contralateral edge correlation is present. Catalog stages include graph analysis and modeling.
summaries.advanced: Improvement is conditional on contralateral edge correlation; the abstract does not quantify gains. Named connectome datasets are not listed here. The method assumes a meaningful left–right split.

plain_language_summary: Left–right pairs of brain cells can be found by matching connection patterns, but earlier tools ignored the wires that cross the midline. This preprint uses those crossing wires too and pairs cells more accurately when the two sides agree.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans head is small enough that optogenetic activation plus whole-brain calcium imaging can measure signal propagation between neuron pairs and test how well anatomy predicts function.
ocar.challenge: Connectomic anatomy may miss extrasynaptic signaling; it was unknown how often evoked dynamics diverge from wired paths.
ocar.action: Randi, Sharma, Dvali and Leifer, in a 2022 paper, systematically measured signal propagation in 23,427 neuron pairs across the C. elegans head by optogenetic activation and whole-brain calcium imaging, including mutant tests of extrasynaptic routes.
ocar.resolution: They report sign, strength, timing, and causal direction of propagation in a functional atlas. Signal propagation differed from anatomical predictions; mutants showed extrasynaptic, dense-core-vesicle-dependent signaling on seconds-or-less timescales, often without a direct wired connection but with relevant peptides and receptors. The functional atlas predicted spontaneous dynamics better than anatomy.
ocar.future_work: They conclude that both synaptic and extrasynaptic signaling drive short-timescale dynamics and that evoked propagation maps are critical for interpreting neural function.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams do not always say how a signal will actually travel. By turning on one worm neuron at a time and watching the rest, this study finds many influences that skip the wired contacts and travel by slower chemical routes.
summaries.intermediate: In 2022, Randi, Sharma, Dvali and Leifer measured 23,427 neuron-pair interactions in the C. elegans head with optogenetics and whole-brain calcium imaging. The resulting atlas of sign, strength, timing, and direction often disagreed with anatomy. Mutants implicated dense-core-vesicle extrasynaptic signaling on seconds-or-less timescales, including pairs without direct synapses. The atlas predicted spontaneous activity better than the connectome. Catalog tags include elegans and DS01 White+.
summaries.advanced: 23,427 pairs is the measured set stated; it is not every possible pair in the worm. Calcium imaging reports somatic transients, not synaptic currents. ‘Better than anatomy’ is a prediction comparison without a numeric score in the abstract. Venue is not listed in the catalog row.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams do not always say how a signal will actually travel. By turning on one worm neuron at a time and watching the rest, this study finds many influences that skip the wired contacts and travel by slower chemical routes.

ocar.opportunity: If proofreading of EM neuron segmentation could be fully automatic, the human detect–classify–correct loop would no longer be required for every error.
ocar.challenge: No existing segmentation is error-free; proofreading is typically interactive. Merge and split errors co-occur and are hard to handle together.
ocar.action: Nguyen, Jeong and colleagues, in a 2021 paper, proposed RLCorrector: hierarchical reinforcement-learning agents that mimic detection, classification, and correction of cell-level segmentation errors, using an episodic setting to treat merge and split errors together.
ocar.resolution: They compare the system with conventional proofreading methods over various testing cases and report efficacy of the fully automatic approach.
ocar.future_work: The hierarchical RL design is offered as a template for automatic proofreading beyond the reported test cases.

summaries.beginner: Computer outlines of cells in electron-microscope images still contain mistakes that people usually fix by hand. This paper trains a set of learning agents to find, classify, and correct those mistakes automatically.
summaries.intermediate: In 2021, Nguyen, Jang, Tuan and Jeong introduce RLCorrector, a hierarchy of reinforcement-learning agents for fully automatic proofreading of EM instance segmentation. Agents specialize in detection, classification, and correction while remaining dependent, and the episodic setting handles concurrent merge and split errors. They report comparisons with conventional proofreading on various tests. Catalog tags include electron microscopy, segmentation, proofreading, and infrastructure. No venue is listed in the catalog row.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not give numeric error reductions. ‘Fully automatic’ still depends on the trained RL policy generalizing to new volumes. Hierarchical task split is a design claim, not an ablation table here.

plain_language_summary: Computer outlines of cells in electron-microscope images still contain mistakes that people usually fix by hand. This paper trains a set of learning agents to find, classify, and correct those mistakes automatically.

ocar.opportunity: A TEM reconstruction of the entire Drosophila larval CNS can reveal synaptic inputs onto neuroendocrine cells, which are well studied as peptide sources but poorly mapped as circuit targets.
ocar.challenge: Sensory and interneuronal pathways that drive neurosecretory outputs, and how they combine, were unclear.
ocar.action: Hückesfeld, Schlegel, Cardona-associated authors and colleagues, in eLife (2021), used the larval whole-CNS TEM reconstruction to map sensory and interneuron inputs to neurosecretory cells projecting to endocrine organs, guided by network modeling.
ocar.resolution: They identify a carbon dioxide–responsive network acting on specific neurosecretory cells, including corazonin and DH44 neurons, and describe combinatorial architecture in which sensory and interneuronal pathways converge onto distinct combinations of neuroendocrine outputs.
ocar.future_work: The combinatorial map is a substrate for testing how internal state and sensory context jointly recruit endocrine combinations.

summaries.beginner: Hormone-releasing brain cells in a fly larva receive specific incoming wiring, not just a fog of chemicals. This paper traces those incoming paths and finds a route that responds to carbon dioxide.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Hückesfeld, Schlegel, Miroschnikow, Schoofs, Zinke, Haubrich, Schneider-Mizell, Truman, Fetter and colleagues map synaptic inputs onto Drosophila larval neuroendocrine cells using a whole-CNS TEM reconstruction (catalog DS03). Network modeling predicts a CO₂-responsive network that includes Crz and Dh44 cells. The architecture is combinatorial: sensory and interneuron paths converge on distinct endocrine combinations. Catalog method is TEM; stage includes acquisition.
summaries.advanced: The CO₂ network is ‘predicted by network modeling’ then identified; the abstract does not separate purely anatomical versus physiologically confirmed edges. Combinatorial convergence is a wiring motif, not a measured endocrine output time series.

plain_language_summary: Hormone-releasing brain cells in a fly larva receive specific incoming wiring, not just a fog of chemicals. This paper traces those incoming paths and finds a route that responds to carbon dioxide.

ocar.opportunity: A terabyte-scale serial-section EM volume of a whole larval zebrafish brain contains more than connectivity: cell morphologies and spatial distributions that a visual analytics system could expose.
ocar.challenge: Most connectomics tooling focuses on reconstructing graphs, not interactive exploration of whole-brain EM with overlaid segmentation and region-wise statistics.
ocar.action: Choi, Hildebrand, Jeong and colleagues, in IEEE Access (2021), introduce ZeVis, combining 2D section views and 3D volumetric visualization with graph-based processing to filter feature segmentations.
ocar.resolution: Applied to a terabyte-scale whole-brain larval zebrafish volume, they analyzed cell-nucleus distributions across anatomical regions using morphological and anatomical filters.
ocar.future_work: The system is offered for statistical comparison of segmented features across regions in other large ssEM brains.

summaries.beginner: A whole baby zebrafish brain imaged in the electron microscope is too large to browse with ordinary tools. This paper describes a viewer that lets scientists look at slices and 3D renderings together and count cell nuclei in chosen regions.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Access (2021), Choi, Hildebrand, Moon, Quan, Tuan, Ko and Jeong present ZeVis for interactive exploration of a terabyte-scale larval zebrafish serial-section EM volume. Linked 2D and 3D views overlay segmentation; a graph-based interface generates filtered feature subsets for regional statistics. They analyze nucleus distributions in anatomical regions. Catalog tags include zebrafish, serial-section EM, sectioning, segmentation, graph analysis, and DS15.
summaries.advanced: The abstract reports a visualization system and a nucleus-distribution analysis, not a complete zebrafish connectome. Terabyte scale is the authors’ data-size statement. Quantitative nucleus results are not numbered here.

plain_language_summary: A whole baby zebrafish brain imaged in the electron microscope is too large to browse with ordinary tools. This paper describes a viewer that lets scientists look at slices and 3D renderings together and count cell nuclei in chosen regions.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans’ known developmental sequence lets connectogenesis—the emergence of the connectome from cell identities, timing, and synapses—be modeled as a competitive process rather than a static adult graph.
ocar.challenge: Relating embryogenetic precursors, connection dynamics, and behavior requires a model of how cells choose synaptic partners over larval time.
ocar.action: Alicea, on bioRxiv (catalog year 2020), uses C. elegans developmental biology to synthesize connectogenesis and demonstrates a first-mover (Stackelberg) model of synaptic connectivity on larval synaptogenesis data.
ocar.resolution: Potential pre- and postsynaptic roles yield heuristic strategies for establishing synapse types. Timing and order of terminal differentiation affect connectivity patterns. The author links small-connectome emergence to behavioral outcomes in animal and in silico models.
ocar.future_work: The opinion piece argues this first-mover view generalizes to other species and developmental systems and can inform simulations of related phenomena.

summaries.beginner: A worm’s wiring diagram grows as cells are born and compete to form contacts. This essay treats that growth as a game of who moves first, and asks how birth order shapes the adult network and behavior.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (catalogued 2020), Bradly Alicea frames C. elegans connectogenesis from embryogenetic precursors through larval synaptogenesis. A first-mover Stackelberg competition model assigns strategies to potential pre- and postsynaptic relationships. He argues timing of terminal differentiation has subtle but consequential effects on connectivity and that small-connectome emergence corresponds to behavioral outcomes. Catalog tags include elegans, modeling, DS01, and neuroAI.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/synthesis with a demonstrated first-mover model, not a new EM reconstruction. Generalization beyond C. elegans is programmatic. Quantitative fit of Stackelberg strategies to synapse counts is not reported in the abstract. Journal field is bioRxiv; uuid is a Frontiers DOI-style identifier in the catalog.

plain_language_summary: A worm’s wiring diagram grows as cells are born and compete to form contacts. This essay treats that growth as a game of who moves first, and asks how birth order shapes the adult network and behavior.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a directed chemical-synapse connectome and neuron-resolved gene expression, so polarity (excitatory versus inhibitory) could be inferred from transmitter–receptor pairs.
ocar.challenge: Graph analyses usually omit connection sign because whole-brain polarity is experimentally hard; no complete sign map existed.
ocar.action: Fenyves, Csermely and colleagues, on bioRxiv (catalog year 2020), predicted signs from presynaptic neurotransmitter and postsynaptic receptor expression covering 3,638 connections and 20,589 synapses, releasing EleganSign.
ocar.resolution: They made successful predictions for more than two-thirds of chemical synapses and report an excitatory:inhibitory ratio of interneuronal ionotropic chemical connections close to 4:1, similar to many real-world networks.
ocar.future_work: They note the method can incorporate spatial and temporal dynamics of polarity, adding plasticity to E:I balance, and is available for any network with an expression atlas.

summaries.beginner: Wiring maps rarely say which contacts excite and which inhibit. Using gene lists for chemical messengers and their receivers in the worm, this study labels most contacts as plus or minus and finds about four exciting connections for each inhibiting one.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (catalogued 2020; PLoS Computational Biology uuid), Fenyves, Szilágyi, Vassy, Sőti and Csermely predict C. elegans chemical-synapse polarity from transmitter and receptor expression (3,638 connections, 20,589 synapses). More than two-thirds of synapses receive predictions; the ionotropic interneuronal E:I ratio is close to 4:1. EleganSign is released. Catalog tags include elegans, graph analysis, and DS01.
summaries.advanced: ‘Successful predictions for more than two-thirds’ is coverage, not a stated accuracy against electrophysiology. The 4:1 ratio applies to interneuronal ionotropic chemical connections as defined by the authors. Binary/incomplete expression atlases can mis-assign sign. Journal field is bioRxiv.

plain_language_summary: Wiring maps rarely say which contacts excite and which inhibit. Using gene lists for chemical messengers and their receivers in the worm, this study labels most contacts as plus or minus and finds about four exciting connections for each inhibiting one.

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila CNS (~150,000 neurons) is near a complete cellular catalogue. Grouping neurons into types (1–1000 cells per hemisphere) is required to parse that complexity, and matched transcriptomes plus morphologies can integrate connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Cell type is a correlation among lineage, expression, morphology, connectivity, physiology, and behavior; matching morphological and transcriptomic definitions brain-wide remains incomplete.
ocar.action: Bates, Janssens, Jefferis and Aerts, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), review how neuroanatomy and gene expression are used to discover fly neuronal types at scale.
ocar.resolution: Initial studies suggest morphological and transcriptomic type definitions are highly consistent. Matched single-cell transcriptomic and morphological data are presented as the reference for integrating other modalities, including connectomes, to improve functional predictions and genetic access.
ocar.future_work: They emphasize remaining work to match approaches brain-wide and to use those matches for connectome interpretation and cell-type manipulation.

summaries.beginner: Even a fruit-fly brain is easier to understand if similar cells are grouped into types. This review explains how cell shape and gene activity are being used together to name those types across the fly nervous system.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Bates, Janssens, Jefferis and Aerts review neuronal cell typing in Drosophila as the adult CNS (~150,000 neurons) nears a complete catalogue. They treat type as co-varying lineage, expression, morphology, connectivity, responses, and behavioral role. Early comparisons find morphological and transcriptomic types highly consistent. Matched atlases are the proposed hub for connectomics and genetic tools. Catalog tags include fly, graph analysis, and cell-types.
summaries.advanced: The ~150,000 neuron figure is the authors’ scale. Consistency of morphology and transcriptome is ‘initial studies,’ not a brain-wide completed match. This is a review, not a new atlas release.

plain_language_summary: Even a fruit-fly brain is easier to understand if similar cells are grouped into types. This review explains how cell shape and gene activity are being used together to name those types across the fly nervous system.

ocar.opportunity: Neurocartography aims to map features from whole-brain projections to synaptic molecules—about 20 orders of magnitude in volume—to explain computation. Light-microscopy strategies can complement EM while full mammalian synaptic brain maps remain distant.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing a complete mammalian brain at synaptic scale may not be feasible for decades, so mesoscale, microscale, and nanoscale organizing principles must come from other methods as well.
ocar.action: Bloss and Hunt, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2019), review existing and emerging neurocartography technologies that complement EM, including array tomography and two-photon serial tomography of the entire mouse brain.
ocar.resolution: They discuss how these tools yield long-range and subcellular synaptic organizing principles and how whole-mouse-brain two-photon tomography can dissect potential connectivity of defined cell types, aiming at a conceptual use of connectomes for circuit function.
ocar.future_work: Principles from these complementary maps are meant to guide how future EM connectomes are interpreted mechanistically.

summaries.beginner: A full wiring diagram of a mammal’s brain at the finest scale is still far off. This review surveys lighter-weight mapping methods that already reveal how connections are organized from whole-brain paths down to individual synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2019), Bloss and Hunt review neurocartography across scales, noting EM has produced complete synaptic maps in some invertebrates but not mammalian whole brains. They highlight light-microscopy approaches including array tomography and two-photon serial tomography of the mouse brain for long-range and subcellular connectivity principles. Catalog tags include mouse, array tomography, two-photon, preparation, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘~20 orders of magnitude’ is the authors’ scale span. The review does not present a new dataset. ‘Potential connectivity’ from two-photon tomography is not synapse-resolved EM. Decade-scale forecasts for full mammalian EM brains are opinions as of 2019.

plain_language_summary: A full wiring diagram of a mammal’s brain at the finest scale is still far off. This review surveys lighter-weight mapping methods that already reveal how connections are organized from whole-brain paths down to individual synapses.

ocar.opportunity: EM, calcium imaging, and X-ray microtomography now produce gigabyte-to-petabyte structural datasets, but many labs lack portable, reproducible pipelines to turn them into connectomes or cell maps.
ocar.challenge: Computer-vision tools are often not scalable or reproducible, blocking extension across experiments.
ocar.action: Johnson, Wilt, Gray-Roncal-associated authors and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2019), built an ecosystem of neuroimaging pipelines with standardized open-source modules, large-scale storage, reproducible algorithms, and workflow engines, demonstrated on EM synapse-level connectomes and X-ray cell distributions.
ocar.resolution: They show that approaches can be standardized across neuroimaging experiments and applied to diverse datasets, with methods intended to transfer to similar problems in other domains.
ocar.future_work: The framework is proposed as a generalized processing layer connecting existing open-source projects for future large neuroimaging volumes.

summaries.beginner: Modern brain images can fill warehouses of hard drives, and many labs cannot easily rerun the same analysis. This preprint packages storage, algorithms, and workflows so large maps of cells and connections can be built in a repeatable way.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Johnson, Wilt, Rodriguez, Norman-Tenazas, Rivera, Drenkow, Kleissas, LaGrow and colleagues describe a reproducible, scalable framework for large neuroimaging datasets. Exemplars estimate synapse-level connectomes from EM and cell distributions from X-ray microtomography. The stack links storage, open algorithms, and workflow engines. Catalog tags include electron microscopy, infrastructure, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: The abstract is a framework paper; quantitative throughput or accuracy on named EM volumes is not given. Domain transfer beyond neuroimaging is suggested, not demonstrated. Reproducibility claims depend on the unspecified module set remaining available.

plain_language_summary: Modern brain images can fill warehouses of hard drives, and many labs cannot easily rerun the same analysis. This preprint packages storage, algorithms, and workflows so large maps of cells and connections can be built in a repeatable way.

ocar.opportunity: Synapse detection in EM should report both cleft location and direction of connectivity, for both vertebrate dyadic and fly polyadic synapses.
ocar.challenge: Most algorithms do not identify location and direction together, and the few that do had not been shown on both dyadic and polyadic synapses.
ocar.action: Parag, Berger, Helmstaedter, Lichtman, Pfister and colleagues, in ECCV Workshops (2018), generate candidates from 3D U-Net signed-proximity predictions, then prune with a second 3D CNN.
ocar.resolution: The method detects cleft and orientation for both dyadic and polyadic synapses and, they report, outperforms existing methods on rodent and fruit-fly brain data. Code is at github.com/paragt/EMSynConn.
ocar.future_work: A single detector for both synapse geometries is intended for mixed connectomics pipelines going forward.

summaries.beginner: Finding a synapse is not enough: one also needs to know which cell is sending and which is receiving. This paper trains two 3D networks to mark the contact and its direction in both mouse-style and fly-style synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In ECCV Workshops (2018), Parag, Berger, Kamentsky, Staffler, Wei, Helmstaedter, Lichtman and Pfister predict signed proximity with a 3D U-Net, then prune candidates with a second CNN to output cleft location and connectivity direction for dyadic and polyadic synapses. They report outperformance on rodent and Drosophila EM. Catalog tags include fly, U-Net, electron microscopy, synapses, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘Outperforms existing methods’ is not accompanied by numeric scores in the abstract. Dyadic versus polyadic performance may still differ even if both are supported. Signed proximity is an intermediate representation whose errors propagate to pruning.

plain_language_summary: Finding a synapse is not enough: one also needs to know which cell is sending and which is receiving. This paper trains two 3D networks to mark the contact and its direction in both mouse-style and fly-style synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Identifying long-range axons from multiple sources inside dense mammalian EM would add color-like identity without chemical conversion or fiducials.
ocar.challenge: EM’s limited color space has made multi-source long-range input labeling notoriously difficult in dense reconstructions.
ocar.action: Drawitsch, Karimi, Boergens and Helmstaedter, in eLife (2018), introduce FluoEM: correlated light and EM imaging with computational matching of neurite reconstructions, virtually labeling axons in dense EM.
ocar.resolution: Fluorescently imaged axons in mouse cortex can be identified in 3D EM once the EM volume is about 40–50 µm in extent, relying on unique axonal trajectories in dense neuropil, exemplified on long-distance input to layer 1.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered for multi-color virtual labeling of long-range axons in other dense cortical EM volumes of sufficient size.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope maps are black-and-white, so axons that came from different distant brain areas look the same. This paper matches glowing light-microscope axons to their electron-microscope shapes so those long-range inputs can be named in the dense map.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2018), Drawitsch, Karimi, Boergens and Helmstaedter present FluoEM, correlating multi-color fluorescence with dense 3D EM without fiducials or chemical conversion. They report faithful axon identification in mouse cortex when EM extent is about 40–50 µm, using unique trajectories, and demonstrate long-distance input into layer 1. Catalog tags include mouse, electron microscopy, and connectomics.
summaries.advanced: The 40–50 µm extent is the authors’ threshold claim. Matching uniqueness may fail for highly parallel or poorly reconstructed axons. The layer-1 example is a demonstration, not a full long-range input census.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope maps are black-and-white, so axons that came from different distant brain areas look the same. This paper matches glowing light-microscope axons to their electron-microscope shapes so those long-range inputs can be named in the dense map.

ocar.opportunity: A 3D U-Net predicting voxel affinities plus simple agglomeration could unify neuron segmentation across isotropic and anisotropic EM if the loss enforces topology.
ocar.challenge: Prior structured losses (MALIS) were computationally heavy (originally O(n²)) and early-training gradients could be spurious; weaker affinity predictions forced complicated agglomeration.
ocar.action: Funke, Tschopp, Saalfeld, Turaga and colleagues, on arXiv (2017), train a 3D U-Net with an O(n log n) MALIS-style structured loss computed in two passes, then iteratively agglomerate regions.
ocar.resolution: Simple agglomeration outperforms more involved methods used on inferior predictions. On CREMI, FIB, and SegEM they report improvements of 27%, 15%, and 250% over previous results, with O(n) runtime and about 2.6 seconds per megavoxel.
ocar.future_work: They suggest a single 3D strategy can serve both isotropic and anisotropic EM and scale to very large datasets.

summaries.beginner: Computers outline neurons by guessing which tiny cubes belong together, then merging them. This paper trains a 3D network with a smarter scoring rule so simple merging works well on several kinds of electron-microscope data.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv.org paper (2017), Funke, Tschopp, Grisaitis, Sheridan, Singh, Saalfeld and Turaga predict affinities with a 3D U-Net trained on a structured MALIS-style loss. They accelerate the gradient to O(n log n) and split it into two passes. On CREMI, FIB, and SegEM, they report 27%, 15%, and 250% improvements over prior results, ~2.6 s/megavoxel, scaling as O(n). Catalog tags include SegEM, U-Net, volume EM, segmentation, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: Percent improvements are relative to unnamed previous results on those three datasets. ‘250%’ is a large relative gain whose baseline is not specified here. Throughput 2.6 s/megavoxel is their figure; hardware is not stated. Two-pass gradients are motivated as avoiding early-training spurious contributions.

plain_language_summary: Computers outline neurons by guessing which tiny cubes belong together, then merging them. This paper trains a 3D network with a smarter scoring rule so simple merging works well on several kinds of electron-microscope data.

ocar.opportunity: Targeted reconstruction of single genetically labeled mammalian neurons, combining confocal arbors with ATUM-SEM synapses, would make large-scale identified-neuron connectomics more feasible.
ocar.challenge: ssEM of mammalian circuits still faces roadblocks that limit general applicability, including finding the same cell from light microscopy in EM.
ocar.action: Hirabayashi, Tapia and Polleux, in Scientific Reports (catalog year 2017), fuse membrane-targeted CAAX-Venus to APEX2, introduce it sparsely into pyramidal neurons by in utero electroporation, and perform Correlated Light-SSEM (CoLSSEM) with confocal then ATUM-SEM.
ocar.resolution: They reconstruct dendritic and axonal arbors in a targeted way and then image ultrastructure and synaptic connections of the same identified neurons.
ocar.future_work: They argue the method will improve feasibility of large-scale reconstructions of identified neurons and of linking ultrastructure to functional or structural connectivity.

summaries.beginner: Researchers tagged individual mouse cortical neurons so they glow under a light microscope and also darken for an electron microscope. That lets the same cell’s branches and synapses be followed without mapping every cell in the volume.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (catalogued 2017), Hirabayashi, Tapia and Polleux express APEX2 fused to CAAX-Venus in sparsely electroporated pyramidal neurons for Correlated Light-SSEM. High-resolution confocal maps arbors; ATUM-SEM then captures ultrastructure and synapses of the same cells. Catalog tags include ATUM, WaferMapper, serial-section EM, CLEM, confocal, sectioning, and acquisition.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not quantify how many neurons or synapses were reconstructed. Extreme sparsity is required for unambiguous LM–EM matching. APEX2 labeling can affect ultrastructure; they present it as retaining quality but do not give a numeric preservation metric here.

plain_language_summary: Researchers tagged individual mouse cortical neurons so they glow under a light microscope and also darken for an electron microscope. That lets the same cell’s branches and synapses be followed without mapping every cell in the volume.

ocar.opportunity: Fly-scale EM volumes are terabytes; distributed segmentation on a cluster could automate tracing if it remains robust to local classifier failures.
ocar.challenge: Datasets exceed single-machine memory. Segmentation errors from poor generalization or image anomalies can ruin a global result if naively merged.
ocar.action: Plaza and Berg, on arXiv (2016), propose a Spark segmentation strategy for very large EM datasets that minimizes disk I/O, is robust to local errors, and uses a plugin architecture with an in-memory segmentation representation.
ocar.resolution: Applied to a few large EM datasets, they report effectiveness and scalability and hope the design will attract external algorithm contributions.
ocar.future_work: The plugin architecture and in-memory representation are meant to host new EM segmentation advances on shared cluster backends.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly electron-microscope volumes are too big for one computer to outline all the cells. This paper splits the job across a cluster in a way that a local mistake is less likely to spoil the whole map.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv.org paper (2016), Plaza and Berg implement large-scale EM image segmentation in Spark, aiming for robustness to classifier errors and image anomalies while reducing disk I/O. They apply the system to large EM datasets and emphasize a plugin architecture plus in-memory segmentation objects. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, segmentation, and proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Named datasets, voxel counts, and accuracy metrics are absent from the abstract. Robustness is a design goal illustrated on ‘a few large EM datasets.’ Spark-era infrastructure predates later cloud-native connectomics stacks.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly electron-microscope volumes are too big for one computer to outline all the cells. This paper splits the job across a cluster in a way that a local mistake is less likely to spoil the whole map.

ocar.opportunity: Complete circuit reconstruction is prohibitively slow when the goal is to compare identified cell types across animals. Genetically driven electron-dense tracers could allow targeted high-resolution reimaging and unsupervised segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Serial-section EM is required for synaptic connectivity, but molecularly selective reconstruction with preserved ultrastructure has been difficult, and imaging everything at high resolution is slow.
ocar.action: Joesch, Mankus, Yamagata, Lichtman, Sanes and colleagues, in eLife (2016), delivered peroxidase derivatives virally to genetically identified neurons and enhanced label electron density while retaining ultrastructure, then combined targeted reimaging with unsupervised segmentation.
ocar.resolution: High contrast enabled selecting regions from a fast low-resolution reconstruction for high-resolution reimaging. They report imaging and reconstruction times reduced by two orders of magnitude, facilitating directed inquiry of circuit motifs.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is intended for comparing neuronal structure and connectivity among multiple animals without full-volume reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Instead of mapping every cell in a chunk of brain, this team darkens only genetically chosen neurons for the electron microscope. They can then zoom in on those cells’ synapses much faster than reconstructing the whole volume.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2016), Joesch, Mankus, Yamagata, Shahbazi, Schalek, Suissa-Peleg, Meister, Lichtman, Scheirer and Sanes use viral peroxidase tracers in genetically identified neurons, with a protocol that boosts electron density while preserving ultrastructure. Contrast supports targeted high-resolution reimaging after a rapid lower-resolution pass and unsupervised segmentation. They report ~100-fold faster imaging and reconstruction. Catalog tags include serial-section EM, sectioning, acquisition, segmentation, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘Two orders of magnitude’ is the authors’ time-reduction claim; absolute hours are not given. Unsupervised segmentation quality is not scored in the abstract. Targeted reconstruction necessarily omits unlabeled partners’ full morphology except at contacts with labeled cells.

plain_language_summary: Instead of mapping every cell in a chunk of brain, this team darkens only genetically chosen neurons for the electron microscope. They can then zoom in on those cells’ synapses much faster than reconstructing the whole volume.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome lets computational ‘attacks’ on neurons and synapses identify which elements are critical for global information-processing properties, informing mixed parallel versus serial circuit design.
ocar.challenge: Functions of every neuron and synapse, and whether behavioral circuits are separate-parallel or integrative-serial, remain unclear.
ocar.action: Kim, Jeong and colleagues, in PLoS Computational Biology (2016), removed 279 neurons and 2,990 weighted connections (6,393 chemical synapses and 890 electrical junctions) in turn and scored effects on global network properties.
ocar.resolution: They identify 12 critical neurons and 29 critical synapses as control elements with the most influence over multiple pathways. Emergent pathways of those synapses support importance of backward locomotion, avoidance, and social feeding; suggest roles for neurons of unclear function; and evidence mixed parallel and serial design.
ocar.future_work: Vulnerability-defined pathways become hypotheses for behavioral and physiological tests of those control elements.

summaries.beginner: If you virtually delete one worm neuron or connection at a time, a few deletions wreck the network’s overall shape. This study lists those critical parts and links them to crawling backward, avoiding things, and social feeding.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2016), Kim, Kim, Kralik and Jeong attack 279 C. elegans neurons and 2,990 weighted connections (6,393 chemical synapses, 890 gap junctions). Twelve neurons and 29 synapses are critical for global information-processing properties and act as control elements. Their synapses form pathways related to backward locomotion, avoidance, and social feeding, and support a mixed parallel/serial architecture. Catalog tags include elegans, graph analysis, and DS01.
summaries.advanced: ‘Critical’ is defined by effects on chosen global network metrics, not by in vivo lesions in this paper. Behavioral labels (backward locomotion, avoidance, social feeding) are interpretations of emergent pathways. Weighted connections combine chemical and electrical edges as specified.

plain_language_summary: If you virtually delete one worm neuron or connection at a time, a few deletions wreck the network’s overall shape. This study lists those critical parts and links them to crawling backward, avoiding things, and social feeding.

ocar.opportunity: Hierarchical segmentation of large 3D EM brain images needs a method whose runtime is quasilinear so whole volumes can be processed.
ocar.challenge: Standard clustering on pixels does not scale; watershed over-segmentation must be merged with affinities that respect object size.
ocar.action: Zlateski and Seung, on arXiv (2015), define a disaffinity graph, over-segment into watershed basins, then merge basins with size-dependent single-linkage clustering on a basin graph.
ocar.resolution: They illustrate the method on 3D electron microscopic brain images and argue quasilinear runtime makes it suitable for large images.
ocar.future_work: The hierarchical basin clustering is offered as a scalable component for EM neuron segmentation pipelines.

summaries.beginner: Big electron-microscope volumes must be chopped into cells without taking forever. This paper first over-divides the image into tiny basins, then glues basins together in a way that depends on their size.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv.org paper (2015), Zlateski and Seung segment images by watershed basins on a disaffinity graph, then apply size-dependent single-linkage clustering on the basin graph. Quasilinear runtime is the scalability claim, illustrated on 3D EM brain images. Catalog tags include structured-loss affinity segmentation, volume EM, segmentation, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: No numeric segmentation scores appear in the abstract. Size-dependent linkage is a heuristic whose bias toward large objects is not quantified here. Illustration on EM is not a named public benchmark.

plain_language_summary: Big electron-microscope volumes must be chopped into cells without taking forever. This paper first over-divides the image into tiny basins, then glues basins together in a way that depends on their size.

ocar.opportunity: Pairs of synapses from one axon onto one dendrite share activity history, so comparing their sizes in EM can bound how finely synaptic strength can be stored.
ocar.challenge: How much information a synapse can store through plasticity is unknown and is limited by variability of size given a shared history.
ocar.action: Bartol, Harris, Sejnowski and colleagues, in eLife (2015), reconstructed hippocampal neuropil and measured spine heads, necks, and lengths for multi-contact pairs from the same axon onto the same dendrite.
ocar.resolution: Spine heads and neck diameters, but not neck lengths, were nearly identical in those pairs. They infer a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths, about 4.7 bits per synapse, with the observed precision requiring averaging activity over several minutes because of stochastic activation.
ocar.future_work: The bound is an upper limit from structural stereotypy under shared history; physiology must test whether that precision is used computationally.

summaries.beginner: When one sending cell makes two contacts onto the same receiving cell, those contacts end up almost the same size. From that sameness, the authors estimate how many distinct ‘strength settings’ a contact could hold.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015), Bartol, Bromer, Kinney, Chirillo, Bourne, Harris and Sejnowski use EM reconstruction of hippocampal neuropil to compare synapses sharing pre- and postsynaptic history. Spine head size and neck diameter, not neck length, are nearly identical in pairs. They estimate at least 26 distinguishable strengths (~4.7 bits) and argue stochastic activation implies averaging over several minutes to reach that precision. Catalog method is electron microscopy.
summaries.advanced: 26 strengths and 4.7 bits are derived from size variability, using the size–efficacy correlation stated in the abstract, not from measured EPSP amplitudes in this paper. ‘Minimum of 26’ is a lower bound on distinguishable levels under their model. Several-minute averaging is an inference from stochastic activation, not a measured integration window.

plain_language_summary: When one sending cell makes two contacts onto the same receiving cell, those contacts end up almost the same size. From that sameness, the authors estimate how many distinct ‘strength settings’ a contact could hold.

ocar.opportunity: A genetically encoded EM synaptic marker would let molecularly defined long-range axons be found in serial-section EM with preserved ultrastructure, enabling connectomics of identified feeding-regulatory cells.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing molecularly defined synapses in ssEM remains challenging despite nanometer resolution.
ocar.action: Atasoy, Betley, Sternson and colleagues, in Nature Neuroscience (2014), developed GESEM, intra-vesicular electron-dense labeling of axonal boutons, usable with Cre or GAL4 in mouse and fly, and applied it to AGRP and POMC hypothalamic neurons.
ocar.resolution: GESEM identified synapses from genetically specified neurons with excellent ultrastructure. Combined with functional and viral mapping, they characterized basic circuit organization of AGRP and POMC axon projections.
ocar.future_work: They present GESEM as enabling long-range connectomics for other molecularly defined cell types.

summaries.beginner: Researchers built a genetic tag that darkens the sending ends of chosen brain cells in electron-microscope pictures. They used it to follow hunger-related cells in the mouse that project far from the hypothalamus.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2014), Atasoy, Betley, Li, Su, Sertel, Scheffer, Simpson, Fetter and Sternson introduce GESEM, a genetically encoded synaptic marker producing intra-vesicular electron-dense label in boutons of Cre- or GAL4-expressing neurons in mouse and fly. Applied to AGRP and POMC cells, selective ultrastructural reconstruction plus functional/viral mapping describes organization of their long-range projections. Catalog tags include mouse, serial-section EM, and sectioning.
summaries.advanced: ‘Excellent preservation of ultrastructure’ is qualitative. Circuit features of AGRP/POMC are ‘some basic features,’ not a complete projection connectome. Dual mouse/fly usability is claimed; the feeding application highlighted is mouse hypothalamus.

plain_language_summary: Researchers built a genetic tag that darkens the sending ends of chosen brain cells in electron-microscope pictures. They used it to follow hunger-related cells in the mouse that project far from the hypothalamus.

ocar.opportunity: Pycnogonids occupy a key position in arthropod evolution; a FIB-SEM connectome of visual neuropils in Achelia langi can be compared with the only other arthropod visual systems reconstructed in comparable detail—crustacean and insect compound eyes.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics had been limited to a few models (mouse, C. elegans, Drosophila). Sea-spider visual circuitry at synapse level was unknown.
ocar.action: Lehmann, Heß, Wanner and Melzer, in BMC Biology (2014), used a FIB-SEM crossbeam workstation to reconstruct the visual connectome of Achelia langi, mapping R-cell targets and synapse signs, with Golgi impregnations for cell-type confirmation.
ocar.resolution: Each hemisphere’s two eyes connect to first and second visual neuropils; the first is split into two hemineuropils, each three-layered. Six postsynaptic neuron types are described (five descending unipolar, one ascending). Mapping chemical synapses indicates descending cells are second-order (postsynaptic to R-cells) while ascending cells are predominantly pre- and sometimes postsynaptic to R-cells (possible feedback). Morphology and synaptic organization resemble crustacean/insect compound-eye systems, so pycnogonid vision shows features of both chelicerate median and mandibulate lateral eyes.
ocar.future_work: The comparison invites further arthropod visual connectomes to test whether these neuron types are homologous or convergent.

summaries.beginner: Sea spiders are distant relatives of insects and spiders, and their tiny visual centers had not been mapped synapse by synapse. This paper does that mapping and finds wiring that looks surprisingly like insect and crustacean eyes in some respects.
summaries.intermediate: In BMC Biology (2014), Lehmann, Heß, Wanner and Melzer reconstruct Achelia langi visual neuropils with FIB-SEM. Two eyes per hemisphere innervate layered first and second neuropils; six neuron types postsynaptic to retinula axons are defined and confirmed with Golgi stains. Synapse mapping assigns descending unipolar neurons as second-order and ascending neurons a possible feedback role. They compare this organization to crustacean and insect compound-eye circuits. Catalog organism/dataset fields list elegans; the abstract is a pycnogonid.
summaries.advanced: Catalog metadata (elegans, DS01) do not match the sea-spider study and should not be used as the biological system. Homology versus convergence with mandibulate visual neurons is an evolutionary interpretation. ‘All identifiable chemical synapses’ is their mapping claim; completeness is not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Sea spiders are distant relatives of insects and spiders, and their tiny visual centers had not been mapped synapse by synapse. This paper does that mapping and finds wiring that looks surprisingly like insect and crustacean eyes in some respects.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation (here, Rhoana) still needs human correction to produce an accurate connectivity map. An open, interactive, scalable annotation tool would make that correction practical.
ocar.challenge: Computer vision results are far from perfect; correcting them on large volumes requires software that scales and stays interactive.
ocar.action: Seymour, Pfister, Lichtman and colleagues, in a 2013 conference paper, present Mojo 2.0, an open-source interactive annotation tool to correct automatic segmentation errors.
ocar.resolution: Mojo 2.0 is offered as the human proofreading interface on top of the Rhoana pipeline for connectome annotation.
ocar.future_work: The tool is intended to support production of accurate connectivity maps from still-imperfect automatic segmentations.

summaries.beginner: Computers sketch the cells in electron-microscope pictures, but people still have to fix the sketch. This 2013 software, Mojo 2.0, is an open tool for making those fixes on large volumes.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2013 conference contribution, Seymour, Mike, Narayanan, Lee, Pfister and Lichtman present Mojo 2.0, an open-source, interactive, scalable annotation tool for correcting automatic EM segmentation (they mention the Rhoana pipeline). The abstract frames it as necessary because fully automatic methods remain imperfect. Catalog tags include electron microscopy, segmentation, proofreading, infrastructure, and graph analysis. No journal name is listed in the catalog row.
summaries.advanced: The abstract is a tool announcement and does not report user-study timing or error-reduction metrics. Dependence on Rhoana is historical. Scalability claims are not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Computers sketch the cells in electron-microscope pictures, but people still have to fix the sketch. This 2013 software, Mojo 2.0, is an open tool for making those fixes on large volumes.

ocar.opportunity: Fly and vertebrate nervous systems share layers, columns, glomeruli, synaptic components, and network features. EM can now determine synaptic circuits cell by cell as part of the fly connectome, while genetics can add function.
ocar.challenge: Bridging structural connectomics to molecular biology and synaptic physiology—so that computation underlying behavior can be read out—remains the hard step.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen and Lee, in Advances in Genetics (2012), review technical advances in functional connectomics in Drosophila: EM circuit mapping, genetic identification of synaptic components, and tools to record and manipulate activity.
ocar.resolution: They offer prognoses for each emerging area and identify challenges in linking structure to molecules and physiology to extract computational mechanisms of behavior.
ocar.future_work: The review’s agenda is that linkage: using genetic physiology on identified connectome pathways to determine fundamental computations.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brains share many design features with ours, and their wiring can be mapped cell by cell. This 2012 review explains the genetic tools that add activity measurements onto that wiring so behavior can be explained.
summaries.intermediate: In Advances in Genetics (2012), Meinertzhagen and Lee review genetic analysis of functional connectomics in Drosophila. They note shared organization with vertebrates and the then-new ability of EM to map synaptic pathways cell by cell. Genetic tools identify synaptic components and manipulate activity. They discuss challenges in bridging structural maps to molecular biology and synaptic physiology. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, and connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2012 review; subsequent whole-brain fly connectomes postdate it. Prognoses in the abstract are qualitative. No new circuit reconstruction is presented.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brains share many design features with ours, and their wiring can be mapped cell by cell. This 2012 review explains the genetic tools that add activity measurements onto that wiring so behavior can be explained.

ocar.opportunity: Nearly isotropic FIB/SEM of adult mammalian cortex lets 3D geometrical features of voxels be used to detect and segment asymmetric, presumed excitatory synapses from sparse interactive labels.
ocar.challenge: Fully automated synapse detection still needed a protocol that exploits high z-resolution and offers 3D proofreading from few training examples.
ocar.action: Kreshuk, Hamprecht and colleagues, in PLoS ONE (2011), trained interactive machine learning on 3D neighborhood geometry in ilastik, then detected and segmented asymmetric synapses in FIB/SEM.
ocar.resolution: On 111 synapses in 409 images (1948×1342 pixels) with three-expert manual annotation, they report 0.92 recall at 0.89 precision, comparable to the experts. Software, test data, and ground truth are released.
ocar.future_work: The public ilastik protocol is meant for other nearly isotropic cortical FIB/SEM volumes with sparse training.

summaries.beginner: In finely sampled 3D electron-microscope stacks, a computer can learn from a few marked synapses what the rest look like. This paper shows that its hit rate on mammalian cortex is about as good as the people who labeled the test set.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2011), Kreshuk, Straehle, Sommer, Köthe, Cantoni, Knott and Hamprecht detect and segment asymmetric (presumed excitatory) synapses in adult mammalian cortex FIB/SEM using interactive ML on 3D geometrical voxel features. Validation on 111 synapses in 409 images with three experts yielded 0.92 recall at 0.89 precision, comparable to experts. ilastik source, data, and ground truth are public. Catalog tags include FIB-SEM, ilastik, sectioning, acquisition, segmentation, and proofreading.
summaries.advanced: The method targets asymmetric/excitatory synapses, not all chemical synapses. Comparability to experts is on this 111-synapse set. Precision/recall pair is one operating point (0.89 / 0.92).

plain_language_summary: In finely sampled 3D electron-microscope stacks, a computer can learn from a few marked synapses what the rest look like. This paper shows that its hit rate on mammalian cortex is about as good as the people who labeled the test set.

ocar.opportunity: The complete C. elegans connectome can be clustered as a directed, weighted network, using bilateral symmetry as a cue, to find modules that match functional circuits and explain cooperation among them.
ocar.challenge: Modular organization of synaptic networks is hard to extract at single-neuron resolution because of connectivity complexity.
ocar.action: Sohn, Jeong and colleagues, in PLoS Computational Biology (2011), applied modularity-based community detection for directed weighted networks to the C. elegans connectome and examined hierarchical topological properties.
ocar.resolution: Incorporating bilateral symmetry, they identified anatomical clusters including a body-spanning cluster that correspond to experimentally identified functional circuits. Hierarchical organization of five clusters is used to explain systemic cooperation (mechanosensation, chemosensation, navigation) among segregated circuits for higher-order behaviors.
ocar.future_work: The five-cluster hierarchy is a hypothesis for how structurally segregated circuits jointly produce complex behavior.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring can be grouped into a handful of communities of tightly linked cells. Those groups line up with known senses and movements, and their stacking may explain how simple circuits work together.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2011), Sohn, Choi, Ahn, Lee and Jeong detect modules in the directed, weighted C. elegans connectome, using bilateral symmetry to assign clusters. Anatomical clusters, including a body-spanning one, match known functional circuits. Five hierarchically organized clusters are proposed to support cooperation among mechanosensory, chemosensory, and navigation circuits. Catalog tags include elegans, graph analysis, and DS01.
summaries.advanced: Correspondence to functional circuits is claimed against experimental identifications not re-demonstrated here. Five clusters is their reported solution; alternative resolutions of modularity are not discussed in the abstract. Bilateral symmetry is a prior that shapes assignment.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring can be grouped into a handful of communities of tightly linked cells. Those groups line up with known senses and movements, and their stacking may explain how simple circuits work together.

ocar.opportunity: A complete larval Drosophila connectome can be run as a frozen rate operator with no fitted single-neuron parameters, then compared with rewired controls to separate what degree and weight statistics fix from what exact wiring fixes.
ocar.challenge: Connectome-constrained models inherit both coarse statistics and exact synapses, so it is unclear which dynamical properties the wiring specifies beyond those statistics.
ocar.action: Therianos, in a 2026 paper, simulated the strongly connected core of 2,825 larval neurons as a leaky-tanh rate operator and compared it with a degree-and-weight-matched rewiring ensemble and further controls.
ocar.resolution: Gross dynamics (non-normal, near-linear; gain and effective dimensionality within a few percent of the ensemble) follow coarse statistics. Sparse afferent drive confines activity to a fifth of the core versus two thirds in the ensemble, and mushroom-body leading modes concentrate far beyond the ensemble—both surviving additional controls and depending on exact synapse placement.
ocar.future_work: The author proposes this decomposition as a general test of whether exact wiring carries information beyond degree and weight statistics when connectivity is used as an architectural prior.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram mixes two kinds of information: how many contacts each cell has, and exactly who talks to whom. This study freezes a larval-fly network into a simple dynamical equation and shows that overall excitability follows the first kind, while where signals travel follows the second.
summaries.intermediate: In 2026, S. Therianos treats the complete larval Drosophila connectome’s strongly connected core (2,825 neurons; catalog DS03) as a frozen leaky-tanh rate operator with no fitted single-cell parameters. Degree-and-weight-matched rewiring accounts for gross non-normal, near-linear behavior (gain and dimensionality within a few percent). Exact wiring confines sparse-drive activity to one fifth of the core (versus two thirds rewired) and concentrates mushroom-body driving modes. Catalog tags include fly, connectome-constrained visual-system model, infrastructure, graph analysis, and modeling. No journal is listed.
summaries.advanced: All properties are attributed to the operator, ‘not a measurement of larval activity.’ ‘A fifth’ versus ‘two thirds’ and ‘a few percent’ are the abstract’s comparisons. The visual-system model method tag may not match this whole-core operator study. Controls (cell-class-preserving, size-matched, singular-subspace, family-wise) are named as surviving tests without full statistics here.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram mixes two kinds of information: how many contacts each cell has, and exactly who talks to whom. This study freezes a larval-fly network into a simple dynamical equation and shows that overall excitability follows the first kind, while where signals travel follows the second.

ocar.opportunity: The nematode esophagus is a feeding organ whose neurons can be compared across free-living C. elegans and P. pacificus and the plant parasite Heterodera glycines to test whether parasitism simplifies synaptic networks.
ocar.challenge: Whether parasite-associated nervous-system simplification is general, and whether it appears at synaptic connectivity, was unclear; neuronal control of cyst-nematode feeding was unknown.
ocar.action: Han, Schroeder and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2026), reconstructed the esophageal connectome of infective second-stage H. glycines juveniles with serial-section EM and compared it with C. elegans and P. pacificus.
ocar.resolution: All three have 20 esophageal neurons with relatively conserved cell-body positions, but H. glycines chemical output to muscle is highly reduced, with gland ensheathment enabling novel synapses, a bias toward monadic synapses, and more neuron–neuron and neuron–gland connections. The network is smaller and less clustered; centrality and synthetic ablation predict different neurons control feeding modules than in free-living species.
ocar.future_work: They identify candidate species-specific circuits for parasite control and show how parasitism can reshape a feeding circuit.

summaries.beginner: A plant-parasitic worm feeds with a piercing spear rather than the pumping throat of a free-living worm. Mapping the feeding-organ nerves shows the same number of cells but far fewer connections onto muscle, and new contacts with gland cells.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Han, Thompson, Conklin, Varshney and Schroeder reconstruct the Heterodera glycines J2 esophageal connectome with ssEM and compare it to C. elegans and Pristionchus pacificus. Twenty neurons and conserved soma positions contrast with reduced motor output, gland ensheathment, monadic-synapse bias, and a smaller, less clustered network. Ablation analysis predicts different control neurons for feeding modules. Catalog tags include elegans, serial-section EM, sectioning, graph analysis, and DS01.
summaries.advanced: Conservation of 20 neurons is a count comparison; synapse-number reductions are qualitative (‘highly reduced’) in the abstract. Catalog DS01/elegans tags the comparison species, not the parasite as the primary reconstruction. Behavioral functions of predicted control neurons are computational, not in vivo lesions.

plain_language_summary: A plant-parasitic worm feeds with a piercing spear rather than the pumping throat of a free-living worm. Mapping the feeding-organ nerves shows the same number of cells but far fewer connections onto muscle, and new contacts with gland cells.

ocar.opportunity: A whole-brain Drosophila connectome lets long-range projections between optic lobes and central brain be classified by polarity and connectivity into feedforward, feedback, and bilateral streams.
ocar.challenge: How early visual pathways interface with brainwide circuits for context-dependent flexibility was not mapped as a three-stream architecture.
ocar.action: Kim and Kim, on bioRxiv (2026), quantified synaptic polarity and connectivity of projection neurons linking the optic lobe reciprocally with the central brain and the contralateral optic lobe.
ocar.resolution: Feedforward neurons form an information bottleneck that consolidates visual features and distributes them modularly. Feedback neurons densely innervate optic-lobe structures via precise recurrent loops. Bilateral neurons link the two optic lobes for inter-ocular processing.
ocar.future_work: The three-stream map is a hypothesis for how context-dependent flexibility enters early vision through identified cell classes.

summaries.beginner: Fly vision is not a one-way street from the eye into the brain. This preprint sorts the long-range visual wires into outgoing, returning, and left–right bridges and describes what each stream is built to do.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Sung Yong Kim and Anmo J. Kim analyze the whole-brain Drosophila connectome for reciprocal optic-lobe–central-brain and contralateral projections. Using polarity and connectivity they define feedforward (bottleneck and modular distribution), feedback (layer-specific recurrent loops), and bilateral (inter-ocular) streams. Catalog organism is fly; dimension is connectomics.
summaries.advanced: Stream labels are anatomical/polarity classifications, not new physiology. ‘Information bottleneck’ is their interpretation of feedforward consolidation. No numeric neuron counts for each stream appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Fly vision is not a one-way street from the eye into the brain. This preprint sorts the long-range visual wires into outgoing, returning, and left–right bridges and describes what each stream is built to do.

ocar.opportunity: Complete fly brain connectomes create an urgent need to assign neuronal cell types from connectivity alone, fast enough for a laptop.
ocar.challenge: Manual or multi-modal typing does not scale to whole-brain wiring diagrams.
ocar.action: Schwartzman, Jourdan, García-Soriano and Matsliah, in Nature Communications (catalog year 2026), introduce NTAC, grouping neurons from synaptic connectivity in semi-supervised (few labels) and unsupervised (no labels) forms.
ocar.resolution: On multiple state-of-the-art fruit-fly brain connectomes, NTAC achieves high accuracy within minutes on a laptop, showing connectivity is a scalable basis for brain-wide type assignment.
ocar.future_work: The method is positioned for automatic typing of further complete connectomes from connectivity graphs alone.

summaries.beginner: Once every connection in a fly brain is listed, computers can sort cells into types using only who talks to whom. This paper’s tool does that quickly on a laptop, with or without a few already-named examples.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (catalogued 2026), Schwartzman, Jourdan, García-Soriano and Matsliah present NTAC (Neuronal Type Assignment from Connectivity). Semi-supervised and unsupervised variants use synaptic connectivity alone. Applied to multiple Drosophila brain connectomes, they report high accuracy in minutes on a standard CPU. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, infrastructure, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘High accuracy’ is not given as a percentage in the abstract. Success on fly brains may not transfer to connectomes without the fly’s stereotyped types. Semi-supervised performance depends on which labels are provided; that sensitivity is not reported here.

plain_language_summary: Once every connection in a fly brain is listed, computers can sort cells into types using only who talks to whom. This paper’s tool does that quickly on a laptop, with or without a few already-named examples.

ocar.opportunity: Fly CNS connectomes usually excise most sensory neurons during preparation. Reconstructing wing sensory axons in FANC and matching them to peripheral organs would close that central–peripheral gap.
ocar.challenge: Without the periphery, wing proprioceptors’ identities, pathfinding, and postsynaptic partners—especially onto steering motor neurons—remain incomplete.
ocar.action: Lesser, Moussa and Tuthill, in eLife (2026), reconstructed wing sensory axons from the Female Adult Nerve Cord EM dataset and mapped them to peripheral structures with genetic tools and light microscopy.
ocar.resolution: They confirm known wing mechanosensory neurons and identify previously uncharacterized axons, including putative proprioceptors with monosynaptic connections onto wing steering motor neurons. Adjacent campaniform sensilla have distinct axon morphologies and partners. Peripheral location and central projections are stereotyped across flies.
ocar.future_work: They offer the atlas and genetic toolkit to guide analysis of other fly connectome datasets.

summaries.beginner: Wiring diagrams of the fly nerve cord often cut off the sensory cells in the wing. This paper traces those wing sensors back into the cord, names new ones, and shows some connect directly to the cells that steer flight.
