summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2026), Lesser, Moussa and Tuthill reconstruct wing sensory axons in FANC (catalog DS07) and match them to peripheral organs with genetics and light microscopy. Known mechanosensors are confirmed; novel putative proprioceptors make monosynaptic contacts onto wing steering motor neurons. Adjacent campaniform sensilla differ in axon shape and partners. Stereotypy across flies is reported. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, preparation, segmentation, synapses, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘Putative proprioceptors’ are identified by anatomy, not new physiology in the abstract. Monosynaptic MN contacts are connectomic. Stereotypy is asserted without a numeric inter-animal variance here.

plain_language_summary: Wiring diagrams of the fly nerve cord often cut off the sensory cells in the wing. This paper traces those wing sensors back into the cord, names new ones, and shows some connect directly to the cells that steer flight.

ocar.opportunity: An EM reconstruction of the predatory nematode Pristionchus pacificus brain, compared with C. elegans after at least 100 million years of divergence, can list anatomical substrates of nervous-system evolution at cellular and subcellular resolution.
ocar.challenge: Understanding bilaterian brain evolution requires precise cellular and subcellular differences, not only gene lists.
ocar.action: Cook, Kalinski, Loer, Hobert-associated authors and colleagues, in 2025 work (Science DOI; catalogued journal bioRxiv), reconstructed the P. pacificus brain with EM and compared it with C. elegans.
ocar.resolution: They report a conserved nematode core connectome plus changes in neuronal cell death, cell position, axo-dendritic projections, and many synaptic changes in homologous neurons whose overall neurite morphology is unchanged. Differences are distributed, including in glia. Some circuit drift leaves behavioral output apparently unaltered.
ocar.future_work: The comparison is offered as a multi-level view of conservation versus change for further evolutionary neuroscience.

summaries.beginner: Two worm species that split long ago still share a core brain wiring plan, but many details have shifted—even in cells that look the same. This reconstruction lists those shifts, including cases where the wiring changed without an obvious change in behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In 2025, Cook, Kalinski, Loer, Memar, Majeed and colleagues reconstruct the Pristionchus pacificus brain by EM and compare it with C. elegans (≥100 million years divergence). A conserved core coexists with changes in cell death, position, projections, and synapses of homologous neurons, distributed across the nervous system and glia, plus examples of circuit drift. Catalog tags include elegans, electron microscopy, graph analysis, and DS01. Journal field is bioRxiv; uuid is a Science DOI.
summaries.advanced: ‘At least 100 million years’ is the authors’ divergence figure. Circuit drift is ‘apparent’ regarding behavioral output. No synapse-count delta is given in the abstract. Catalog journal bioRxiv versus Science DOI should be noted when citing.

plain_language_summary: Two worm species that split long ago still share a core brain wiring plan, but many details have shifted—even in cells that look the same. This reconstruction lists those shifts, including cases where the wiring changed without an obvious change in behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes of three Caenorhabditis species can map which neuronal identities are conserved and which signaling pathways diverge over more than 45 million years.
ocar.challenge: Brain evolution at single-neuron-class resolution across entire nervous systems had not been charted this way.
ocar.action: Toker, Ben-David and colleagues, in Current Biology (2025), generated whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes for three Caenorhabditis species and compared neuronal classes.
ocar.resolution: Neuronal-cell-type identities are remarkably stable; combinatorial homeodomain transcription-factor expression is among the best classifiers of homologous classes. Transmitter-producing neuron identities remain stable, but ionotropic and metabotropic receptor expression diverges so that more than half of neuron classes change their capacity to receive specific transmitters. Neuropeptide and receptor expression also diverge while dense wireless network topology stays stable. Small secreted proteins unlike conventional neuropeptides show similarly cell-type-specific, evolvable expression.
ocar.future_work: They propose these patterns as candidate principles for how evolutionary novelty arises in neuronal circuits.

summaries.beginner: Across related worm species, the named neuron types stay recognizable, but the chemical locks and keys they use drift. More than half of cell types change which messengers they can listen to, even if they still make the same messengers themselves.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2025), Toker, Ripoll-Sánchez, Geiger, Sussfeld, Saini, Beets, Vértes, Schafer and Ben-David compare whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes of three Caenorhabditis species (>45 million years). Type identity is stable and well classified by homeodomain codes. Glutamate, acetylcholine, GABA, and monoamine neuron identities hold, but receptor expression shifts in more than half of classes. Neuropeptidergic graphs remain dense while nodes change. Catalog tags include elegans, graph analysis, and DS01.
summaries.advanced: ‘More than half of all neuron classes’ changing receptive capacity is the headline quantitative claim. Transmitter identity stability versus receptor divergence is transcriptomic, not physiological confirmation of sign. Novel small secreted proteins are candidates, not proven transmitters. Connectome tags reflect C. elegans as the anatomical reference, not new EM.

plain_language_summary: Across related worm species, the named neuron types stay recognizable, but the chemical locks and keys they use drift. More than half of cell types change which messengers they can listen to, even if they still make the same messengers themselves.

ocar.opportunity: The femoral chordotonal organ is the largest somatosensory organ in the Drosophila leg and has been proposed to encode both joint proprioception and substrate vibration. Downstream EM connectivity can split those functions.
ocar.challenge: Which FeCO sensory neurons and central circuits serve internal versus external sensing was unknown.
ocar.action: Lee, Dallmann, Tuthill, Agrawal and colleagues, in Nature Communications (2025), reconstructed and analyzed circuits downstream of the FeCO using EM connectomics (catalog DS07 VNC).
ocar.resolution: Position- and movement-encoding FeCO neurons connect to local VNC leg motor circuits (proprioceptive). Vibration-encoding neurons are integrated across legs and sent to mechanosensory brain regions (exteroceptive). The split matches a broader invertebrate/vertebrate theme of specialized vibration pathways.
ocar.future_work: They argue connectivity is a powerful way to assign putative internal versus external functions of somatosensory neurons more generally.

summaries.beginner: Sensors in a fly’s leg report both the leg’s own motion and vibrations from the ground. Following their wires shows those two jobs are split: one path stays in the nerve cord to help control the leg, the other is shared across legs and sent up to the brain.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2025), Lee, Dallmann, Cook, Tuthill and Agrawal use EM connectomics of Drosophila FeCO downstream circuits. Position/movement afferents feed local VNC motor control; vibration afferents are integrated across legs and projected to brain mechanosensory regions. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, DS07 VNC, and connectomics.
summaries.advanced: Function (proprioceptive versus exteroceptive) is inferred from connectivity plus prior encoding classes, not new recordings in the abstract. Cross-species vibration-pathway homology is a literature framing. Completeness of FeCO reconstruction is not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Sensors in a fly’s leg report both the leg’s own motion and vibrations from the ground. Following their wires shows those two jobs are split: one path stays in the nerve cord to help control the leg, the other is shared across legs and sent up to the brain.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila head-direction circuit is a sensitive test of whether a measured connectome, plus modest cell-type-level parameter fits, can recover continuous attractor dynamics that integrate velocity.
ocar.challenge: Continuous attractors theoretically need finely tuned wiring, but connectomes are variable and omit synaptic gains, thresholds, and time constants.
ocar.action: Duan, Dong and Fiete, on bioRxiv (2025), combined self-supervised and unsupervised objectives to estimate unknown parameters at cell-type (not synapse) resolution from the raw HD connectivity matrix.
ocar.resolution: The recovered network robustly exhibits continuous attractor dynamics and integrates a range of velocity inputs despite departures from an idealized ring. They characterize how connectome deviations shape viable solutions and use in-silico ablations to assign cell-type roles.
ocar.future_work: They argue connectome-derived structure plus minimal biologically grounded tuning can replicate known physiology and elucidate function in other circuits.

summaries.beginner: A fly’s internal compass is thought to need very precise wiring, but real wiring diagrams are messy and missing many electrical details. This preprint fills in a few type-level knobs and still gets a working compass that integrates motion.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2025), Duan, Dong and Fiete estimate cell-type-level parameters on the Drosophila head-direction connectome with mixed self-supervised and unsupervised objectives. The resulting network shows continuous attractor dynamics and velocity integration despite biological irregularity versus a ring attractor. Ablations probe cell-type roles. Catalog tags include fly, connectome-constrained visual-system model, electron microscopy, graph analysis, and modeling.
summaries.advanced: Parameters are fit at cell-type, not individual synapse, resolution. ‘Robustly exhibits’ attractor dynamics is a simulation result, not new physiology. The visual-system model method tag may be inherited catalog metadata rather than the HD circuit itself. Solution-space characterization with respect to connectome deviations is not numeric here.

plain_language_summary: A fly’s internal compass is thought to need very precise wiring, but real wiring diagrams are messy and missing many electrical details. This preprint fills in a few type-level knobs and still gets a working compass that integrates motion.

ocar.opportunity: EPG heading neurons integrate visual input from ER neurons of the anterior visual pathway. Densely reconstructing every AVP neuron from EM can predict which visual features and spatial regions feed navigation.
ocar.challenge: How visual information is encoded and integrated by the navigation system remains incompletely understood.
ocar.action: Garner, Kind, Rubin, Wernet-associated authors and colleagues, in Nature (2024), densely reconstructed all neurons in the Drosophila AVP from EM, classifying MeTu, TuBu, and ER stages and MeTu subtypes by morphology, connectivity, and synapse location, then predicted ER visual features from AVP connectivity and MeTu dendritic fields, confirming some predictions physiologically.
ocar.resolution: Four MeTu types further split into ten subtypes by medulla synapses and AOTU targets define distinct information channels. The reconstruction predicts visual features and visual area supplying any ER neuron, providing a foundation for how features are transformed into higher-order cognitive representations.
ocar.future_work: Unconfirmed physiological predictions of ER feature selectivity are the next measurements.

summaries.beginner: Flies keep track of heading using visual clues, but the exact pictures those compass cells receive were unclear. Mapping every cell in the visual path to the compass lets researchers predict what each compass input sees, and some of those predictions already match recordings.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Garner, Kind, Lai, Nern, Zhao, Houghton, Sancer, Wolff, Rubin, Wernet and colleagues densely reconstruct the Drosophila anterior visual pathway (medulla → AOTUsu → bulb → ER → EPG). Four MeTu types and ten subtypes define channels; connectivity plus dendritic fields predict ER visual features and spatial sampling, with some physiological confirmation. Catalog tags include fly, electron microscopy, and connectomics.
summaries.advanced: ‘All neurons in the AVP’ is the authors’ completeness claim. Ten MeTu subtypes are defined by pre- and postsynaptic patterns stated in the abstract. Physiological confirmation is partial (‘some of these predictions’). Feature inference assumes connectivity and dendritic fields suffice without full biophysics.

plain_language_summary: Flies keep track of heading using visual clues, but the exact pictures those compass cells receive were unclear. Mapping every cell in the visual path to the compass lets researchers predict what each compass input sees, and some of those predictions already match recordings.

ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide calcium in behaving animals contains time-varying communities. Unsupervised affinities plus tensor factorization and weighted community detection could yield a dynamic functional connectome aligned to experimental stages.
ocar.challenge: Static synaptic connectivity contrasts with changing participation of neurons in behavior; extracting which communities form when is non-trivial.
ocar.action: Dyballa, Zucker and colleagues, at ICLR (2024), compute pairwise nonlinear affinities among neuronal traces, organize them with non-negative tensor factorization, then apply a generative weighted community-detection model.
ocar.resolution: Each factor specifies which neurons interact in an inferred interval and in which animals. Time codes experimental variables, producing an atlas of motifs during stimuli or spontaneous behaviors. They report experimental validation that the method predicts causal interactions generating behavior.
ocar.future_work: The pipeline is offered for other brain-wide calcium datasets where a dynamic functional connectome is needed.

summaries.beginner: The same brain cells team up in different groups at different moments. This paper learns those shifting teams from activity recordings and checks that the predicted influences actually help generate behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In ICLR (2024), Dyballa, Lang, Haslund-Gourley, Yemini and Zucker learn dynamic affinities from brain-wide calcium in behaving animals via non-negative tensor factorization, then weighted community detection. Factors mark interacting neuron groups over inferred intervals and animals, yielding motif atlases by experimental stage. They report experimental validation of predicted causal interactions. Catalog tags include segmentation and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: ‘Experimentally validated’ causal prediction is asserted without a metric in the abstract. NTF communities are functional, not synaptic. Catalog segmentation tag may not match the functional-connectome focus. Organism is not named in the catalog row.

plain_language_summary: The same brain cells team up in different groups at different moments. This paper learns those shifting teams from activity recordings and checks that the predicted influences actually help generate behavior.

ocar.opportunity: As connectomics outpaces physiology, interpreting a wiring diagram to predict function becomes a primary mode of investigation. The Drosophila optic lobe is a test case for predicting form-vision roles from connectivity.
ocar.challenge: Structure is known in far more detail than function; theoretical predictions must be specific enough to test.
ocar.action: Seung, in Nature (2024), analyzed Drosophila optic-lobe structure to predict that three Dm3 and three TmY types participate in form vision, inferring classical and extraclassical receptive fields from connectivity and conjecturing downstream conjunctions/disjunctions of oriented features.
ocar.resolution: Predicted receptive fields suggest local orientation encoding; extraclassical fields have implications for robust orientation tuning, position invariance, and illusory-contour completion. TmY types synapse onto optic-lobe projection neurons hypothesized to compute logical combinations of oriented features.
ocar.future_work: Predictions are to be tested with neurophysiology, which would constrain parameters and biophysical mechanisms in neural-network models of fly vision.

summaries.beginner: Sometimes we know a brain’s wiring better than what the cells do. This paper reads the fly visual wiring and predicts that certain cells detect the tilt of edges in a scene, a guess meant to be tested with recordings.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), H. S. Seung interprets a Drosophila optic-lobe wiring diagram to predict form-vision functions for three Dm3 and three TmY cell types. Connectivity-derived receptive fields suggest local orientation encoding; extraclassical fields are linked to robust tuning, position invariance, and contour completion. TmY outputs onto projection neurons are conjectured to compute conjunctions and disjunctions of oriented features. Catalog tags include fly, graph analysis, and modeling.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical interpretation, not new physiology. ‘Three Dm3 and three TmY’ types are specified; receptive-field predictions assume connectivity-to-function mappings that physiology must constrain. Extraclassical implications (illusory contours, invariance) are conjectural.

plain_language_summary: Sometimes we know a brain’s wiring better than what the cells do. This paper reads the fly visual wiring and predicts that certain cells detect the tilt of edges in a scene, a guess meant to be tested with recordings.

ocar.opportunity: The retina’s compact networks are an ideal model for rules of neural-network construction. High-resolution EM connectomics can reveal topologies behind retinal computations and how they develop or fail in disease.
ocar.challenge: How retinal computations are implemented in allowable networks still needs anatomical maps to constrain models.
ocar.action: Sigulinsky, Pfeiffer and Jones, in Annual Review of Vision Science (2024), review retinal connectomics findings on cells, connectivity organization, development, and disease.
ocar.resolution: They survey how EM datasets map specific cells and connectivities and argue that anatomy-informed modeling has been and will remain instrumental in understanding visual-signal processing in the retina.
ocar.future_work: Continued use of these maps to inform models of development and disease is the stated trajectory.

summaries.beginner: The retina is a small, layered network that does the first steps of seeing. This review collects what fine-scale wiring maps have taught us about those steps, and how the wiring is built or breaks.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Vision Science (2024), Sigulinsky, Pfeiffer and Jones review retinal connectomics: EM mapping of cells and connectivity, developmental shaping, and breakdown in disease. They emphasize the retina as a model for network construction and the role of anatomical maps in modeling visual computations. Catalog tags include mouse, electron microscopy, graph analysis, and DS09/DS10 mouse retina.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new volume. Catalog mouse-retina tagging reflects the dominant EM resources discussed, not a single dataset paper. Disease and development sections are surveys.

plain_language_summary: The retina is a small, layered network that does the first steps of seeing. This review collects what fine-scale wiring maps have taught us about those steps, and how the wiring is built or breaks.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing Drosophila leg and wing premotor connectomes in the same animal can reveal shared modular logic and specializations reflecting different biomechanics and evolutionary origins.
ocar.challenge: How premotor networks let individual muscles contribute to many behaviors, and whether recruitment rules differ between legs and wings, was unknown at synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Lesser, Azevedo, Phelps and colleagues, in Nature (2024), used connectomics to analyze wiring logic of premotor circuits controlling Drosophila leg and wing motor neurons.
ocar.resolution: Both networks cluster into modules linking motor neurons of related muscle functions. In most leg modules, premotor synaptic weights scale with target motor-neuron size, a basis for hierarchical recruitment. Wing premotor networks lack proportional connectivity, which may allow more flexible recruitment of steering muscles.
ocar.future_work: The comparison isolates common organizational principles versus specializations to test in physiology and in other motor systems.

summaries.beginner: Walking and flying use different muscles but both need premotor networks that group related muscles. In the fly, leg networks look set up to recruit larger cells more strongly, while wing-steering networks look more freely mixed.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Lesser, Azevedo, Phelps, Elabbady, Cook, Syed, Mark, Kuroda and colleagues compare Drosophila leg and wing premotor connectomes. Both cluster into modules of functionally related motor neurons. Most leg modules show premotor weights proportional to motor-neuron size (hierarchical recruitment); wing networks lack that proportionality, possibly enabling flexible steering-muscle recruitment. Catalog organism is fly.
summaries.advanced: Proportionality of weights to MN size is a connectivity pattern, not a measured recruitment order in this abstract. ‘Most’ leg modules is the authors’ qualifier. Evolutionary-origin interpretations are comparative framing. Completeness of premotor coverage is not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Walking and flying use different muscles but both need premotor networks that group related muscles. In the fly, leg networks look set up to recruit larger cells more strongly, while wing-steering networks look more freely mixed.

ocar.opportunity: Precise adult connectivity coexists with the observation that neurons taken out of context readily form unspecific synapses. Viewing development through synaptic promiscuity can explain how genomes encode wiring.
ocar.challenge: Many experiments perturb development genetically and score synapses only in the adult, obscuring when specificity was imposed—before, during, or after the moment of choice.
ocar.action: Wolterhoff and Hiesinger, in Current Biology (2024), review experimental evidence for promiscuous synapse formation and the sequential mechanisms that restrict partners.
ocar.resolution: They argue promiscuity at the moment of choice can be required for precision, flexibility, and robustness, depending on how much prior development restricts available partners and how much later development corrects synapses. Specificity is algorithmic: neurons capable of promiscuous synaptogenesis are continuously prevented from wrong choices; no single mechanism or time point suffices.
ocar.future_work: They urge experiments that time-resolve when defects arise rather than reading only adult connectivity after developmental perturbation.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells can make sloppy contacts if you take them out of their usual neighborhood, yet adult brains look precisely wired. This review argues that sloppiness during development is not a failure—it is part of how precision is achieved and kept flexible.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2024), Wolterhoff and Hiesinger review synaptic promiscuity in brain development. Specificity is the outcome of processes before, during, and after synapse formation. Adult-only scores after developmental genetic perturbation often cannot say when a mechanism acted. They conclude that promiscuous competence plus continuous restriction, not a single recognition code or time point, explains precise connectivity. Catalog tags include synapses and neuroanatomy.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review, not a new connectome. The ‘algorithmic process’ framing is interpretive. Evidence that promiscuity is necessary rather than merely tolerated is drawn from the cited literature, not a single experiment reported here.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells can make sloppy contacts if you take them out of their usual neighborhood, yet adult brains look precisely wired. This review argues that sloppiness during development is not a failure—it is part of how precision is achieved and kept flexible.

ocar.opportunity: The forthcoming adult Drosophila central brain connectome (>125,000 neurons, 50 million synapses) plus neurotransmitter identity can drive a whole-brain leaky integrate-and-fire model of feeding and grooming.
ocar.challenge: Whether connectivity and predicted transmitters suffice to describe complete sensorimotor transformations, including shared sugar/water appetitive paths, was untested at this scale.
ocar.action: Shiu, Sterne and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2023), built a whole-brain LIF model and tested predictions with calcium imaging, optogenetics, and behavior.
ocar.resolution: Gustatory activations predicted taste-responsive, feeding-required neurons and motor-neuron firing (optogenetically validated). Taste-class interactions and a partially shared sugar/water appetitive pathway were predicted and confirmed. Mechanosensory activations predicted a non-overlapping antennal grooming set and subtype responses.
ocar.future_work: The preprint is the modeling counterpart later published in Nature (2024); remaining work is expanding behaviors beyond feeding and grooming.

summaries.beginner: This preprint is a whole-fly-brain computer model built only from wiring and predicted chemical identities. It guesses how taste and touch turn into feeding or grooming, and several guesses were confirmed in real flies.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Shiu, Sterne, Spiller, Franconville and colleagues simulate the entire adult Drosophila brain as leaky integrate-and-fire units from connectivity and neurotransmitter identity. Predictions cover feeding initiation, motor firing, aversive/appetitive taste interactions, a shared sugar/water pathway (confirmed with calcium imaging and behavior), and antennal grooming. Catalog tags include fly and modeling.
summaries.advanced: This preprint closely matches the later Nature paper in the same shard; treat them as versions of one modeling project. Transmitter identity is predicted. Validation is for selected circuits, not the full 125,000-neuron dynamics.

plain_language_summary: This preprint is a whole-fly-brain computer model built only from wiring and predicted chemical identities. It guesses how taste and touch turn into feeding or grooming, and several guesses were confirmed in real flies.

ocar.opportunity: About 8% of Drosophila Kenyon cells receive predominantly visual input, but their tuning was poorly understood. FlyWire can list those visual inputs and test whether sampling is random and combinatorial like olfaction.
ocar.challenge: Visual Kenyon-cell input diversity, spatial sampling, and expansion-coding properties relative to olfactory Kenyon cells were unclear.
ocar.action: Ganguly, Heckman, Litwin-Kumar, Clowney and Behnia, in 2023 work (Nature Communications DOI; catalogued journal bioRxiv), used the FlyWire adult whole-brain connectome to identify inputs to visual Kenyon cells.
ocar.resolution: Input types are similar across hemispheres and connectomes, with certain inputs highly overrepresented. Many visual projection neurons sample large visual space; local interneurons contribute smaller, more spatially restricted fractions. Visual Kenyon cells receive sparse mixed inputs from multiple optic-lobe neuropils, consistent with random sampling of available inputs—sparse, distributed, combinatorial coding—but expansion properties differ because a specific visual repertoire meets relatively few visual Kenyon cells.
ocar.future_work: Different expansion coding versus olfaction is a hypothesis for how visual memories are represented in the mushroom body.

summaries.beginner: A minority of the fly’s memory cells get visual rather than smell inputs. Mapping those visual wires shows each memory cell samples a sparse mix of visual channels, similar in spirit to smell coding but with a smaller expansion.
summaries.intermediate: In 2023, Ganguly, Heckman, Litwin-Kumar, Clowney and Behnia use FlyWire (catalog DS06) to map inputs to Drosophila visual Kenyon cells (~8% of KCs). Visual projection neurons often have large fields; local interneurons are more restricted. Sparse combinatorial inputs from multiple optic neuropils match random sampling. Expansion coding differs from olfaction because few visual KCs meet a specific input repertoire. Catalog tags include fly and FlyWire. Journal field is bioRxiv; uuid is Nature Communications.
summaries.advanced: The 8% figure is from the abstract. Random-sampling consistency is a statistical claim without a p-value here. ‘Highly overrepresented’ inputs are not listed by name in the abstract. Cross-connectome similarity is asserted qualitatively.

plain_language_summary: A minority of the fly’s memory cells get visual rather than smell inputs. Mapping those visual wires shows each memory cell samples a sparse mix of visual channels, similar in spirit to smell coding but with a smaller expansion.

ocar.opportunity: Cell-to-cell connectivity matrices from volume EM hide circuit motifs unless rows and columns are reordered—for example to separate feedback from feedforward relative to information flow.
ocar.challenge: Existing discrete reordering algorithms become unsatisfying at large circuit size or scale poorly in CPU time.
ocar.action: Borst and Denk, on bioRxiv (2023), assign each cell a real-valued ‘smooth-index’ location and minimize a cost continuously rather than by discrete permutations.
ocar.resolution: They find the smooth-index algorithm outperforms compared methods, including topological sorting, in both performance and computing-time scaling.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered for detecting assemblies and quantifying feedback in growing connectomic matrices.

summaries.beginner: A table of who connects to whom only reveals patterns if the rows are sorted well—for example so forward wires sit on one side of the diagonal. This preprint sorts the table by sliding cells along a smooth line instead of swapping them one by one.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Borst and Denk reorder connectome matrices by optimizing a continuous index per cell (‘smooth-index’) rather than discrete permutations. The goal includes separating feedforward and feedback relative to information flow and revealing assemblies. They report better performance and scaling than compared algorithms, including topological sorting. Catalog tags include volume EM, graph analysis, and acquisition.
summaries.advanced: No numeric runtime or quality scores appear in the abstract. Success depends on the chosen cost function, which is not specified here. Volume-EM catalog tags reflect intended use, not a new EM volume.

plain_language_summary: A table of who connects to whom only reveals patterns if the rows are sorted well—for example so forward wires sit on one side of the diagonal. This preprint sorts the table by sliding cells along a smooth line instead of swapping them one by one.

ocar.opportunity: The whole-brain fly connectome specifies paths but not whether or how neurons affect each other in vivo. Combining stochastic optogenetic perturbations with a connectome prior could estimate a causal ‘effectome’ efficiently.
ocar.challenge: A causal dynamical model of an entire brain has seemed out of reach; measuring every pairwise effect is infeasible without exploiting anatomy.
ocar.action: Pospisil, Aragon, Dorkenwald, Matsliah, Schlegel and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2023), propose a statistical estimator that uses perturbation data for causal effects and the connectome as a prior, then analyze the connectome to find circuits with greatest total effect on dynamics.
ocar.resolution: Dominant circuits significantly involve only relatively small, often anatomically localized neuron populations, making imaging and stimulation feasible. The approach rediscovers known circuits and generates testable dynamical hypotheses. They argue global fly-brain dynamics are generated by many small circuits operating largely independently.
ocar.future_work: That modular picture implies a causal model of a brain may be feasible in the fly by targeting those small populations.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram says who could influence whom, not who actually does. This preprint outlines a plan to poke fly neurons at random, read the effects, and use the wiring as a hint so a causal map of the brain might be finished in practice.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Pospisil, Aragon, Dorkenwald, Matsliah, Sterling, Schlegel, Yu, McKellar, Costa and colleagues define an ‘effectome’ estimator combining stochastic optogenetic perturbations with a connectome prior. Connectome analysis finds that circuits with greatest total dynamical effect involve relatively small neuron populations, often localized; known circuits are rediscovered. They infer that global dynamics are a collection of largely independent small circuits. Catalog dimension is connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods-and-analysis proposal plus connectome-based circuit ranking; the abstract does not report a completed whole-brain effectome dataset. ‘Relatively small populations’ is not a neuron count. Independence of circuits is an inference from the ranking, not a full causal partition.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram says who could influence whom, not who actually does. This preprint outlines a plan to poke fly neurons at random, read the effects, and use the wiring as a hint so a causal map of the brain might be finished in practice.

ocar.opportunity: Accurate neuronal-structure segmentation in anisotropic EM would reduce manual labeling for micro-connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Enormous variety of neuronal structures makes segmentation among the hardest connectome-reconstruction tasks.
ocar.action: Xiao, Han and colleagues, in Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine (2022), proposed a deep residual contextual and subpixel convolution network, with lifted multicut post-processing, for anisotropic EM stacks.
ocar.resolution: On the ISBI EM segmentation challenge they report a Rand score of 0.98788 (top of the leaderboard). On public mouse piriform cortex they report Rand scores of 0.9562 and 0.9318 on different testing stacks, described as significantly improved over state-of-the-art.
ocar.future_work: They present the automatic method as an effective approach for neuroanatomists to obtain segmentation and reconstruction of neurons.

summaries.beginner: Outlining twisted nerve-cell shapes in electron-microscope stacks is one of the hardest computer-vision jobs in brain mapping. This paper’s network scores very highly on a public contest and on mouse cortex test stacks.
summaries.intermediate: In Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine (2022), Xiao, Hong, Liu, Tang, Xie and Han segment neuronal structures in anisotropic EM with a residual contextual and subpixel-convolution network, then lifted multicut. ISBI challenge Rand score is 0.98788; mouse piriform cortex test stacks score 0.9562 and 0.9318. Catalog tags include mouse, electron microscopy, and segmentation.
summaries.advanced: Rand scores are the abstract’s metrics; other error types (split/merge) are not listed. ‘Top of the leaderboard’ is as of this paper’s ISBI result. Piriform scores are on two unnamed testing stacks.

plain_language_summary: Outlining twisted nerve-cell shapes in electron-microscope stacks is one of the hardest computer-vision jobs in brain mapping. This paper’s network scores very highly on a public contest and on mouse cortex test stacks.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans connectomes at nanoscale let adjacency versus selective partnership (Peters’ rule versus chemoaffinity) be tested as predictors of synapses.
ocar.challenge: Whether neurons synapse indiscriminately with neighbors (Peters’ rule) or choose among adjacent cells with a molecular code remained unresolved.
ocar.action: Cook, Kalinski and Hobert, on bioRxiv (2022), evaluated the expansive set of C. elegans connectomes, modeling synaptic connectivity as a path-length-dependent process of neuronal adjacency and brain strata.
ocar.resolution: They find synaptic connectivity can be accurately modeled from adjacency and strata, offering strong support for Peters’ rule as an organizational principle of C. elegans brain wiring.
ocar.future_work: The result is a C. elegans-specific organizational claim; testing whether lock-and-key selection dominates in other species is left open.

summaries.beginner: Do worm neurons connect to whoever they touch, or do they pick favorites among neighbors? This preprint finds that how close cells are, and which layer they sit in, already predicts most of the wiring.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2022), Cook, Kalinski and Hobert test Peters’ rule against chemoaffinity using C. elegans connectomes. Modeling synapses as a path-length-dependent function of adjacency and brain strata accurately accounts for connectivity, supporting neighborhood as a primary predictor. Catalog tags include elegans, segmentation, synapses, and DS01.
summaries.advanced: ‘Accurately modeled’ is not a numeric score in the abstract. Support for Peters’ rule in C. elegans does not refute molecular codes that act by positioning processes. Multiple connectome versions are ‘the expansive set’; which reconstructions are not listed here.

plain_language_summary: Do worm neurons connect to whoever they touch, or do they pick favorites among neighbors? This preprint finds that how close cells are, and which layer they sit in, already predicts most of the wiring.

ocar.opportunity: The larval Drosophila connectome and single-cell genetics make the giant GABAergic APL neuron a precise test of how sparsening relates to associative olfactory memory—and whether APL activation can itself reinforce.
ocar.challenge: APL’s structure, polarity, connectivity, and metamorphic development needed a detailed account; a rewarding effect of activating an inhibitory neuron would be unexpected.
ocar.action: Mancini, Thoener, Schleyer-associated authors and colleagues, in Journal of Neuroscience (2022), combined behavioral and connectomic analyses, optogenetics, Ca²⁺ imaging, and pharmacology on larval APL.
ocar.resolution: They provide a detailed structural and connectivity account and confirm that APL activation inhibits mushroom-body Kenyon cells, consistent with sparsening. Surprisingly, pairing APL activation with odor establishes an odor-specific appetitive short-term memory without changing naive olfactory behavior. Acute dopamine-synthesis inhibition and pPAM ablation impair that APL-driven reward learning.
ocar.future_work: They suggest a previously unrecognized capacity of central-brain GABAergic neurons to engage dopaminergic reinforcement, as a case of complex function in a numerically simple brain.

summaries.beginner: A huge inhibitory cell in the fly larva’s memory center normally quiets other cells so smells stay distinct. Turning that cell on together with a smell can still teach the larva to like the smell, and that lesson needs dopamine.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2022), Mancini, Thoener, Tafani, Pauls, Mayseless, Strauch, Eichler, Champion, Kobler, Weber and colleagues study larval Drosophila APL with connectomics (catalog DS03), optogenetics, calcium imaging, and pharmacology. APL inhibits Kenyon cells, matching a sparsening role. Optogenetic APL activation paired with odor creates appetitive short-term memory; naive olfaction is unaffected. Dopamine synthesis blockade and pPAM ablation impair the APL-driven reward. Catalog organism is fly.
summaries.advanced: Rewarding capacity is optogenetic, not a claim that APL is a natural reward neuron in all tasks. Dependence on pPAM dopamine is loss-of-function evidence in the abstract without effect sizes. Sex of larvae is noted as either. Journal is Journal of Neuroscience; uuid is a bioRxiv-style DOI in the catalog.

plain_language_summary: A huge inhibitory cell in the fly larva’s memory center normally quiets other cells so smells stay distinct. Turning that cell on together with a smell can still teach the larva to like the smell, and that lesson needs dopamine.

ocar.opportunity: Given a recurrent network’s synaptic connectivity matrix, stored attractor memories might be reconstructed if the inference problem is theoretically possible and a practical algorithm exists.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics raises the open question of when stored information can be recovered from wiring alone, versus remaining unidentifiable.
ocar.action: Goldt, Krzakala, Zdeborová and Brunel, in PLoS Computational Biology (catalog year 2021), determine when reconstruction is theoretically possible in specific attractor models and provide an approximate Bayesian algorithm inspired by statistical physics, analyzed exactly and compared with PCA.
ocar.resolution: They study performance on three models, compare with standard algorithms such as PCA, and explore limitations of reconstructing stored patterns from synaptic connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The theory and algorithm are a template for asking the same identifiability question of empirical connectomes under explicit storage assumptions.

summaries.beginner: If memories live in the strengths of connections, can you read the memories back out from a wiring table? This paper says when that is even possible in simple network models and gives a method that tries to do it.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (catalogued 2021), Goldt, Krzakala, Zdeborová and Brunel study Bayesian reconstruction of patterns stored in attractor networks from the connectivity matrix. They give conditions for theoretical possibility, an approximate Bayesian algorithm from statistical physics (amenable to exact analysis), tests on three models, and comparisons to PCA, plus limitations. Catalog tags include graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: Results are on specified attractor models, not a biological connectome. ‘Three models’ are not named in the abstract. Limitations of reconstruction are flagged as part of the contribution; numeric recoverability thresholds are not given here.

plain_language_summary: If memories live in the strengths of connections, can you read the memories back out from a wiring table? This paper says when that is even possible in simple network models and gives a method that tries to do it.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila’s mushroom body is richly innervated by dopaminergic neurons and now sits in a whole-brain synaptic connectome, making it a system to study how dopamine integrates external, internal, and learned information for flexible behavior.
ocar.challenge: How signals for state- and context-dependent decisions are integrated and modulated, and how heterogeneous dopaminergic populations contribute beyond reward learning, is poorly understood.
ocar.action: Siju, De Backer and Grunwald Kadow, in Cell and Tissue Research (2021), review dopamine modulation of sensory processing and adaptive behavior in flies, emphasizing mushroom-body dopaminergic innervation.
ocar.resolution: They survey evidence that dopaminergic neurons integrate sensory information, internal and behavioral states, and learned experience, and that the mushroom body uses that innervation to modulate decision-making by context and state.
ocar.future_work: The fly connectome and genetic access are presented as the way to dissect heterogeneous dopaminergic roles in adaptive behavior.

summaries.beginner: Dopamine is famous for teaching animals about rewards, but in flies it also helps mix what is happening now, how the animal feels, and what it has learned. This review focuses on those broader jobs in fly sensory circuits and a memory center.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell and Tissue Research (2021), Siju, De Backer and Grunwald Kadow review dopamine in Drosophila sensory processing and adaptive behavior. They note dopaminergic heterogeneity beyond associative reward learning and the mushroom body’s dense dopaminergic innervation as an integrator of multimodal, state, and memory information for decisions. Catalog tags include fly and connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; no new circuit reconstruction is presented. Heterogeneity of dopaminergic neurons is a literature synthesis. Connectome availability is a framing as of 2021.

plain_language_summary: Dopamine is famous for teaching animals about rewards, but in flies it also helps mix what is happening now, how the animal feels, and what it has learned. This review focuses on those broader jobs in fly sensory circuits and a memory center.

ocar.opportunity: Hierarchical clustering of huge supervoxel graphs for 3D EM segmentation needs a distributed algorithm whose result equals processing the whole image at once.
ocar.challenge: Interfaces between regions can span arbitrarily many chunks, so naive chunked clustering would depend on the chunking scheme when scores are statistics of affinities along an interface.
ocar.action: Lu, Zlateski and Seung, on arXiv (2021), recursively cluster in doubling chunks, delaying merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries until a later round when they lie fully inside a chunk.
ocar.resolution: The final clustering is provably independent of chunking and identical to unchunked processing. They demonstrate clustering of an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels from a 3D EM brain image.
ocar.future_work: The chunked exact clustering is intended as production infrastructure for still-larger EM affinity graphs.

summaries.beginner: Gluing tiny pieces of a gigantic brain image into cells has to be split across computers, but the answer must not depend on how you slice the job. This paper delays some gluing decisions until a piece sits fully inside one computer’s share, and proves the result matches doing it all at once.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv.org paper (2021), Lu, Zlateski and Seung distribute hierarchical clustering of supervoxels by recursive doubling chunks, postponing merges that touch boundaries. The result is provably chunking-independent. They cluster >1.5 trillion edges among 135 billion supervoxels from 3D EM brain imagery. Catalog tags include volume EM, segmentation, and graph analysis.
summaries.advanced: 1.5 trillion edges and 135 billion supervoxels are the scale figures. Mean/median interface scores are the example statistics that make naive chunking incorrect. No segmentation accuracy metric is given—this is a systems/algorithm result.

plain_language_summary: Gluing tiny pieces of a gigantic brain image into cells has to be split across computers, but the answer must not depend on how you slice the job. This paper delays some gluing decisions until a piece sits fully inside one computer’s share, and proves the result matches doing it all at once.

ocar.opportunity: T4/T5 axons terminate in four lobula-plate layers encoding cardinal motion directions. A 3D EM reconstruction of their synaptic partners can show how ON and OFF pathways converge and how new directions and lobula projections arise.
ocar.challenge: Input circuitry of T4/T5 is well studied, but synaptic connectivity of circuits integrating their motion signals was largely unknown.
ocar.action: Shinomiya, Nern, Meinertzhagen, Plaza and Reiser, on bioRxiv (2021), comprehensively identified T4/T5 synaptic partners in the lobula plate from a 3D EM reconstruction.
ocar.resolution: ON and OFF pathways converge: same-layer T4 and T5 connect to common partners with similar weights and form a core motif with bilayer interneurons (motion opponency). Pathways likely encode new directions by integrating vertical and horizontal T4/T5 signals. Substantial projections into the lobula suggest directionally selective signals shape feature detection there. New cell types and new patterns on known types are reported.
ocar.future_work: The map extends known motion pathways for experimental and computational analyses toward complete sensory-motor routes.

summaries.beginner: Fly motion sensors dump their signals into a layered brain region, but who listens next was incomplete. This reconstruction lists those listeners, shows how bright-edge and dark-edge paths join, and finds routes that may compute diagonal motions and send motion cues onward.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Shinomiya, Nern, Meinertzhagen, Plaza and Reiser reconstruct T4/T5 partners in the Drosophila lobula plate. Same-layer T4 and T5 share partners symmetrically and participate in a bilayer-interneuron motif for motion opponency. Integrating vertical and horizontal channels likely yields new directions; projections into lobula may shape feature detection. Catalog tags include fly, volume EM, synapses, graph analysis, and neuroanatomy.
summaries.advanced: ‘Comprehensively identified’ is the authors’ completeness language. Symmetric similar weights are qualitative in the abstract. New motion directions are ‘likely’ from anatomy, not new physiology. Lobula projections are a hypothesis about feature detection.

plain_language_summary: Fly motion sensors dump their signals into a layered brain region, but who listens next was incomplete. This reconstruction lists those listeners, shows how bright-edge and dark-edge paths join, and finds routes that may compute diagonal motions and send motion cues onward.

ocar.opportunity: Handling 10²–10³ serial sections (‘mesoscale’ batches) between cutting and imaging is a bottleneck for ssEM connectomics. In-line trapping with 100-µm repeatability would enable robotic pickup onto imaging substrates.
ocar.challenge: Delicate sections in the 10⁰–10⁶ range are hard to transport and position accurately; mesoscale batches lack a reliable automated handler.
ocar.action: Lee, Forest and colleagues, in eNeuro (2020), built a section-handling device interfacing with a conventional ultramicrotomy diamond knife, with a mathematical model of capillary and Stokes forces.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate exact-constraint trapping at 100-µm repeatability and automated handling of eight datasets of 126 serial sections onto EM and light-microscopy substrates with average loss rate 0.50% and throughput 63 s/section, without significant defects.
ocar.future_work: The system is framed as automated mesoscale serial sectioning for scalable 3D-EM connectomics.

summaries.beginner: After a diamond knife cuts a ribbon of brain slices, someone still has to catch and place each slice for imaging. This device traps slices in the water boat with high repeatability so a robot can pick them up, losing about one in two hundred.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2020), Lee, Yip, Kumar, Lewallen, Bumbarger, Reid and Forest present capillary- and Stokes-based trapping of serial sections at an ultramicrotome knife, with 100-µm repeatability. A model of water–air interface forces accompanies the device. Eight automated datasets of 126 sections each went onto EM and LM substrates at 0.50% average loss and 63 s/section. Catalog tags include serial-section EM, sectioning, and infrastructure.
summaries.advanced: 100 µm, 0.50%, 63 s/section, n = 8 datasets of 126 sections are the abstract’s figures. ‘Without significant defects’ is their quality claim. The model ‘fundamentally extends’ water–air interface modeling as stated by the authors. Mesoscale here means 10²–10³ sections, not mesoscale tracing in the neuroanatomical sense.

plain_language_summary: After a diamond knife cuts a ribbon of brain slices, someone still has to catch and place each slice for imaging. This device traps slices in the water boat with high repeatability so a robot can pick them up, losing about one in two hundred.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM of apical tufts between cortical layers 1 and 2, across four mouse cortical regions, can test whether inhibitory innervation at the main bifurcation and distal tuft is cell-type specific among L2, L3, and L5 pyramids.
ocar.challenge: Connectomic principles for controlling pyramids at their apical dendrites, and whether inhibitory axons prefer L2 versus L3/5 tufts, were unclear.
ocar.action: Karimi, Odenthal, Drawitsch, Boergens and Helmstaedter, in eLife (2020), applied 3D EM to apical tufts in four mouse cortical regions and compared inhibitory versus excitatory input by pyramidal type.
ocar.resolution: Relative inhibitory input at the main bifurcation is more than 3-fold stronger for layer 2 pyramids than for all other pyramids. Toward distal tufts in upper layer 1, relative inhibition is about 2-fold stronger for L5 pyramids. Only L3 pyramids show homogeneous inhibitory density. Inhibitory axons preferentially innervate either L2 or L3/5 apical dendrites, not both.
ocar.future_work: These ratios point to differential computation in L2, L3, and L5 pyramids and to type-specific inhibitory control in upper layers.

summaries.beginner: The tufted tops of cortical cells receive a mix of go and stop contacts that depends on which layer the cell lives in. Layer 2 cells are especially strongly inhibited at a main branch point, while layer 5 cells are more inhibited farther out; different inhibitory axons choose one group or the other.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Karimi, Odenthal, Drawitsch, Boergens and Helmstaedter use 3D EM (catalog volume EM) in four mouse cortical regions to quantify innervation of pyramidal apical tufts. L2 pyramids have >3-fold stronger relative inhibition at the main bifurcation than other pyramids; L5 pyramids have ~2-fold stronger relative inhibition in upper layer 1 distal tufts; L3 is homogeneous. Inhibitory axons prefer L2 or L3/5 tufts, not both. Catalog organism is mouse.
summaries.advanced: Fold-changes (>3-fold, ~2-fold) are the abstract’s ratios of relative inhibitory input. Four cortical regions are pooled as ‘across all cortices’ for the main claims. ‘Preferentially innervated either L2 or L3/5, but not both’ is an axonal targeting rule, not a complete inhibitory-cell-type census.

plain_language_summary: The tufted tops of cortical cells receive a mix of go and stop contacts that depends on which layer the cell lives in. Layer 2 cells are especially strongly inhibited at a main branch point, while layer 5 cells are more inhibited farther out; different inhibitory axons choose one group or the other.
